title: distributions explainer
text:
ImportantMy questions about Bayesian workflow



To make predictions with a Bayesian model, is it okay to look at the mean of the raw data to set my priors? Or is it better not to look at the raw data’s summary?

Looking at the mean of the predictor variables is generally fine, especially while you’re learning. The important distinction is:
✅ Using data summaries to set weakly informative priors (reasonable boundaries)
❌ Using data summaries to set very tight priors that essentially “peek” at the answer

Log-Normal Distribution

# | echo: false
# These two are identical:
rlnorm(N, 0, 1)
exp(rnorm(N, 0, 1))


Practical Intuition
Since rnorm(N, 0, 1) gives values mostly between -2 and +2, after exp() that becomes roughly 0.14 to 7.4 — a huge range for a slope

\(e^2 \approx 7.4\)

With rnorm(N, 0, 0.5), values are mostly between -1 and +1, so after exp() you get roughly 0.37 to 2.7 — much more controlled.

\(e^2 \approx 2.7\)



Sample and Plot

# Try different SD values and see what slopes you get
b1 <- rlnorm(1000, 0, 1)    # original
b2 <- rlnorm(1000, 0, 0.5)  # tighter
b3 <- rlnorm(1000, 0, 0.25) # very tight

par(mfrow=c(1,3))
hist(b1, main="SD=1", xlim=c(0,10))
hist(b2, main="SD=0.5", xlim=c(0,10))
hist(b3, main="SD=0.25", xlim=c(0,10))

Then ask yourself: does a slope of 7 make sense? (Ch4.7 Hard Qs example: That would mean every 1 kg of weight adds 7 cm of height — probably too steep for children)

title: Ch3: Sampling the Imaginary
text:
Common example when teaching Bayesian statistics intro:
Pr_Positive_Vamp <- 0.95
Pr_Positive_mortal <- 0.01
Pr_Vamp <- 0.001
Pr_Positive <- Pr_Positive_Vamp * Pr_Vamp + Pr_Positive_mortal * (1- Pr_Vamp )

(Pr_Vamp_Positive <- (Pr_Positive_Vamp * Pr_Vamp)/Pr_Positive)

[1] 0.08683729
Not intuitive: Whenever the condition of interest is very rare, having a test that finds all the true cases is still no guarantee that a positive result carries much info at all. Reason being: most positive results - false positives.
Again, though, not inherently Bayesian - just uses the theorem. Since all the probabilities are about the frequencies of events, rather than theoretical parameters, all major stat philosophies agree to use Bayes’ theorem in this case.
Frequency format: Posed in a way that’s more intuitive..
If we test all 100,000 people, what proportion of those who test positive for vampirism truly vampires? Now, just count up the positive testers: 95 + 999 = 1094. Of the 1094, 95 are real vamps, so
\[Pr(vampire|positive) = 95/1094 \approx 0.087\]
Exploiting frequency bias for predicting things with posterior distributions!

title: SR_Ch03_notes
text:
Common example when teaching Bayesian statistics intro:

Pr_Positive_Vamp <- 0.95
Pr_Positive_mortal <- 0.01
Pr_Vamp <- 0.001
Pr_Positive <- Pr_Positive_Vamp * Pr_Vamp + Pr_Positive_mortal * (1- Pr_Vamp )

(Pr_Vamp_Positive <- (Pr_Positive_Vamp * Pr_Vamp)/Pr_Positive)

[1] 0.08683729


Not intuitive: Whenever the condition of interest is very rare, having a test that finds all the true cases is still no guarantee that a positive result carries much info at all. Reason being: most positive results - false positives.
Again, though, not inherently Bayesian - just uses the theorem. Since all the probabilities are about the frequencies of events, rather than theoretical parameters, all major stat philosophies agree to use Bayes’ theorem in this case.
Frequency format: Posed in a way that’s more intuitive..

In a population of 100,000 people, 100 are vampires.
Of the 100 vampires, 95 will test positive for vampirism.
Of the 99,900 mortals, 999 will test positive for vampirism.

If we test all 100,000 people, what proportion of those who test positive for vampirism truly vampires? Now, just count up the positive testers: 95 + 999 = 1094. Of the 1094, 95 are real vamps, so
\[Pr(vampire|positive) = 95/1094 \approx 0.087\]
Exploiting frequency bias for predicting things with posterior distributions!

Instead of integral calculus, we’ll just sample parameter values from the probability distributions. This turns it into a problem of data summary (a frequency format).

Inside a computer, parameters are just as empirical as outcome of coin flip or die toss.
Empirically attack the posterior








Note



Scientific inference often framed:

An hypothesis is either T or F
We use statistical procedure and get imperfect cue of hypothesis’ falsity
We (should) use Bayes’ Theorem to logically deduce the impact of the cue on our uncertainty

Toy example to see how little statistical procedures can do for us: Suppose the probability of a positive finding, when a hypothesis is true, is Pr(sig|true) = 0.95. This is the power of the test. Suppose the probability of a positive finding, when a hypothesis is false, is Pr(sig|false) = 0.05. That’s the false-positive (Type II Error) rate, like the 5% of conventional significance testing. Finally, we have to state the base rate at which hypotheses are true. Suppose for example that 1 in every 100 hypotheses turn out to be true. Then Pr(true) = 0.01. No one knows this value, but the history of science suggests it’s small (very few long-standing true hypotheses). Now use Bayes’ to compute the posterior:
\[Pr(true|pos) = \frac{Pr(pos|true)Pr(true)}{Pr(pos)} = \frac{Pr(pos|true)Pr(true)}{Pr(pos|true)Pr(true) + Pr(pos|false)Pr(false)}\]
Answer is approx 0.16. A positive finding corresponds to true hypothesis only 16% of the time. Same low base-rate phenomenon that applies in medical testing. Can shrink the false-positive rate to 1% and get the posterior prob up to 0.5, only as good as coin flip.
The most important thing to do is improve Pr(true), the base rate… just come up with a better hypothesis = thinking, not testing!





p_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1000)
prob_p <- rep(1, 1000)
prob_data <- dbinom(6, 9, prob=p_grid) #likelihood p^L * (1-p)^W
posterior <-  prob_data * prob_p #unstandardized posterior 
posterior <- posterior/sum(posterior) # standardized

plot(p_grid, posterior, type="l")








Draw 10,000 samples from this posterior. Imagine the posterior is a bucket filled with parameter values (the \(p\)s, like 0.25, 0.1, 0.93, 0.5, 1, etc.). Within the bucket, each value exists in proportion to its posterior probability, such that values near the peak are much more common than those in the tails. Scoop out 10,000 values. Provided the bucket is well mixed, the resulting samples will have the same proportions as the exact posterior density. Therefore, the individual values of \(p\) will appear in our samples in proportion to the posterior plausibility of each value.
sample pulls values from vector randomly.

samples <- sample(p_grid, prob=posterior, size=1e4, replace=TRUE)
plot(samples)








In this plot, it’s like you’re flying over the posterior distribution, looking down at it. There are many more samples from the dense region near 0.6 and few samples below 0.25.

dens(samples)








dens function from the rethinking library computes the density estimate from the samples and plots it against the proportion of water (p).
Estimated density is similar to ideal posterior in 3.2.



Now, use samples to describe and understand the posterior. How it’s summarized depends on research goals. Common questions:

How much posterior probability lies below some parameter value?
How much posterior probability lies between two parameter values?
Which parameter value marks the lower 5% of the posterior probability?
Which range of parameter values contains 90% of the posterior prob?
Which parameter value has the highest posterior probability?

Three types of questions: (1) intervals of defined boundaries, (2) Intervals of defined probability mass, and (3) Point estimates.


What’s the posterior prob that the proportion of water is less than 50%?
Ok, without using the samples, we can easily calculate this with the grid-approx posterior:

sum(posterior[p_grid < 0.5])

[1] 0.1718746


This is easy with one parameter examples. But if there’s more parameters, will get more complicated. That’s when we’d use the sampling method to describe the data. So take the sum of sampled parameter values that are less that 0.5 divided by 10000 (the frequency).

sum(samples < 0.5) / 1e4

[1] 0.1725


Also get how much post prob lies between 0.5 and 0.75:

sum(samples > 0.5 & samples < 0.75) / 1e4

[1] 0.6065





Getting the integral. Usually known as confidence interval. He calls it Compatibility interval. it is a range of parameter values compatible with the model and data.
Easier to do this with sampling method than the computed grid-approximate posterior distribution.
Find boundaries of lower 80% posterior probability:

quantile(samples, 0.8)

      80% 
0.7577578 


Middle 80% interval is between the 10th percentile and 90th percentile:

quantile(samples, c(0.1,0.9))

      10%       90% 
0.4484484 0.8118118 


Percentile intervals: communicate the shape of distribution, given that the distribution is not too asymmetrical. But imperfect when trying to support inferences about which parameters are consistent with data.
Consider observing 3 Ws in 3 tosses and uniform(flat) prior:

p_grid <- seq(0,1,length.out=1000)
prior <- rep(1, 1000)
likelihood <- dbinom(3, 3, prob=p_grid)
posterior <- prior * likelihood 
posterior <- posterior / sum(posterior)
samples <- sample(p_grid, size=1e4, replace=TRUE, prob=posterior)

PI(samples, prob=0.5)

      25%       75% 
0.7064565 0.9299299 


PI(samples, prob) from the rethinking package computes the central percentile compatibility interval
Highly skewed, its max value is at the boundary of p=1 (right end of x-axis). The percentile interval misses the skewed shape of the posterior.
In contrast, use the highest posterior density interval (HPDI): the narrowest interval containing the specified probability mass. Want the interval with the parameter vals most consistent with the data = densest of intervals.

HPDI(samples, prob = 0.5)

     |0.5      0.5| 
0.8378378 0.9989990 


This interval captures the parameters w/ highest posterior prob, and is noticeably narrower: 0.16 in width compared to the 0.23 for the PI.
Benefits of HPDI is mostly seen when the posterior is highly skewed. When the posterior is bell shaped, it shouldn’t matter which interval type you use.

p_grid <- seq(0,1,length.out=1000)
prior <- rep(1, 1000)
likelihood <- dbinom(6, 9, prob=p_grid)
posterior <- prior * likelihood 
posterior <- posterior / sum(posterior)
samples <- sample(p_grid, size=1e4, replace=TRUE, prob=posterior)

PI(samples, prob=0.5)

      25%       75% 
0.5455455 0.7397397 



HPDI(samples, prob = 0.5)

     |0.5      0.5| 
0.5705706 0.7627628 


Disadvantages of HPDI: more computationally intensive, suffers greater simulation variance (sensitive to how many samples are drawn from the posterior)






Note



Overall, if the choice of interval type makes a big difference, then you shouldn’t be using intervals to summarize the posterior. Remember, the entire posterior distribution is the Bayesian “estimate.” It summarizes the relative plausibilities of each possible value of the parameter. Intervals of the distribution are just helpful for summarizing it. If choice of interval leads to different inferences, then you’d be better off just plotting the entire posterior distribution.





Bayesian estimate is the entire posterior distribution. Producing point estimates often discards information.
Can get the highest post probability - maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. Using 3W in 3 tosses example:

p_grid[which.max(posterior)]

[1] 0.6666667


Or from the samples from the posterior:

chainmode(samples, adj=0.01)

[1] 0.6614294


Why mode verses posterior mean or median?

mean(samples)

[1] 0.6383389

median(samples)

[1] 0.6466466


Loss function: rule that displays the cost associated with using any particular point estimate

Different loss functions imply different point estimates

Heuristic vignette: Tell me which value of p, the proportion of water on the Earth, you think is correct. I will pay you $100, if you get it exactly right. But I will subtract money from your gain, proportional to the distance of your decision from the correct value. Precisely, your loss is proportional to the absolute value of d−p, where d is your decision and p is the correct answer.

We could change the precise dollar values involved, without changing the important aspects of this problem. What matters is that the loss is proportional to the distance of your decision from the true value.

Calculating expected loss for any given decision - use posterior to average over our uncertainty in the true value. Don’t know the true value, so use entire posterior distribution.
Suppose decision, p=0.5. Expected loss will be

sum(posterior * abs(0.5 - p_grid))

[1] 0.1640626


Compute the weighted average loss, where each loss is weighted by its corresponding posterior probability.
Trick to compute for every possible decision: sapply

loss <- sapply(p_grid, function(d) sum(posterior * abs(d- p_grid)))
# loss contains all possible decision loss values. we want to find the value that minimizes the loss
p_grid[which.min(loss)] # gets the index of the min value, finds correspoding val on p_grid

[1] 0.6446446


Which is the posterior median: the parameter value that splits the posterior density such that half the mass is above it and below it.

median(samples)

[1] 0.6466466


Different loss functions nominate diff point estimates. Two common ones:

Absolute loss - median as point estimate
Quadratic loss (d-p)^2 - posterior mean

When posterior distribution is symmetrical and normal-looking - mean and median converge






Note



Usually, research scientists don’t think about loss functions. And so any point estimate like the mean or MAP that they may report isn’t intended to support any particular decision, but rather to describe the shape of the posterior. You might argue that the decision to make is whether or not to accept an hypothesis. But the challenge then is to say what the relevant costs and benefits would be, in terms of the knowledge gained or lost. Usually it’s better to communicate as much as you can about the posterior distribution, as well as the data and the model itself, so that others can build upon your work. Premature decisions to accept or reject hypotheses can cost lives.

title: Ch3: Sampling the Imaginary
text:
Sampling to simulate prediction
Likelihood functions work in both directions: given a realized obs, the likelihood function says how plausible the obs is. Given only parameters, the likelihood defines a distribution of possible obs that we can sample from to simulate obs. = generative models simulate predictions
dummy data: simulated data in generative models
Globe-tossing example. Two tosses: three possible observations (0 W, 1W, 2W). Compute probability for each, for any value of prior p.

# p = 0.7 
dbinom(0:2, size=2, prob=0.7)

[1] 0.09 0.42 0.49


0W: 9%; 1W: 42%, 2W: 49%
Simulate observations using these probabilities.

# r for random binomial, (# of simulations, size of N tosses, prob)
rbinom(1, size=2, prob=0.7)

[1] 2

rbinom(10, size=2, prob=0.7)

 [1] 1 2 1 2 2 1 2 2 2 1



dummy_w <- rbinom(100000, size=2, prob=0.7)
table(dummy_w)/1e5

dummy_w
      0       1       2 
0.08980 0.42023 0.48997 



dummy_w <- rbinom(1e5, size=6, prob=0.7)
simplehist(dummy_w, xlab = "dummy water count")








Model checking: (1) ensuring the model fitting worked correctly, (2) evaluating the adequacy of a model for some purpose

Software working correctly? Retrodictions ask how well the model reproduces the data used to educate it
Model adequacy? All models are false, so we’re not testing whether the “truthiness” of the model;s assumptions. We’re trying to assess exactly how the model fails to describe the data, as a path toward model comprehension, revision, and improvement

Typically hope to either predict future observations or understand enough that we might usefully tinker with the world


Implied predictions in models are uncertain in two ways:

Observation uncertainty: for any unique value of the parameter p, there is a unique implied pattern of observation the model expects (garden of forking data). Uncertainty in predicted observations, because even if you know p with certainty, you won’t know the next globe toss with certainty (unless p=0 or 1).
Prior uncertainty, embodied by the posterior distribution. Everything depends on p - so uncertainty extends outward, affecting the sampling variation.

Need to propagate the parameter uncertainty when evaluating implied predictions. So over the posterior density for p, compute predictions for each value of p. - average all these prediction distributions together to get the posterior predictive distribution.



w <- rbinom(1e4, size=9, prob=0.6)
simplehist(w)








This generates 1e4 simulated predictions of 9 globe tosses assuming p = 0.6. The predictions are stored as counts of water. Theoretical min = 0; max = 9.
To propagate the parameter uncertainty into these predictions: replace the value 0.6 with samples from the posterior

w <- rbinom(1e4, size=9, prob=samples)
simplehist(w)








samples is the same list of random samples from the posterior distributions used before. For each sampled value, a random binomial observation is generated.

Combine simulated observation distributions for all parameter values, each weighted by its posterior prob → posterior predictive distribution

Propagates uncertainty about parameter to uncertainty about prediction

Can manipulate these simulated observations just like you can manipulate samples from the posterior (compute intervals, point estimates)

The simulated model predictions are quite consistent with the observed data in this case - the actual count of 6 lies right in the middle of the simulated distribution. Quite a bit of spread to predictions, but this spread arises from the binomial process itself, not uncertainty about p. Still premature to conclude the model is perfect. Questionable assumption in the independence of globe tosses.

title: Ch 4: Geocentric Models
text:
Ptolemy is often ridiculed for his geocentric model of the solar system, but he was mathematically brilliant. He computed an accurate model of the motions of the planets (epicycles - accurate from the earthly perspective, would just have to be re-calibrated every 100 years). Makes useful predictions given narrow domain of questioning. = Generalized system of approximation (Fourier series).
Linear regression is the geometric model of applied statistics. Linear regression: family of simple golems attempting to learn about the mean and variance of some measurement using an additive combinations of other measurements


Which uses a Gaussian (normal) distribution to describe our golem’s uncertainty about some measurement of interest.
Binomial distribution models the number of discrete successes (k) in a fixed number (n) of independent binary trials (Y/N, T/F). As the number of trials becomes large, the binomial distribution approaches the continuous Gaussian distribution, which is characterized by a bell-shaped curve defined by its mean and SD.


Random walks on a soccer field.

pos <- replicate(1000,sum(runif(16,-1,1)))
plot(density(pos))








INC number of steps INC stabilization on the Gaussian distribution. Any process that adds together random values from the same distribution converges to normal. Fluctuations from the mean cancel themselves out - most likely sum is sum in which every fluctuation is canceled by another (sum of zero)

Regardless of underlying distribution




Another way to get normal distribution.

prod(1+runif(12,0,0.1))

[1] 1.899116



Samples 12 random numbers between 1.0 and 1.1, each representing a proportional increase in growth. The product of all 12 is computed and returned.


growth <- replicate(1e4, prod(1 + runif(12,0,0.1)))
dens(growth, norm.comp=TRUE)








The effect at each locus was multiplied by the effects at all the others, NOT ADDED. Normal distribution because the effect at each locus is SMALL (multiplying small numbers is approx same as addition).






Note



Small effects that multiply together are approximately additive, so they tend to stabilize on Gaussian distributions



big <- replicate(1e4, prod(1+runif(12,0,0.5)))
small <- replicate(1e4, prod(1 + runif(12,0,0.01)))
dens(big, norm.comp=TRUE)







dens(small, norm.comp=TRUE)












log.big <- replicate(1e4, log(prod(1+runif(12,0,0.5))))
dens(log.big, norm.comp=TRUE)








Adding logs is equivalent to multiplying the original numbers. Measurement scales are arbitrary, and it’s natural to measure sound, earthquakes, information on a log scale.




Ontological reason: World full of Gaussian distributions: measurement errors, variations in growth, velocities of molecules.
Processes that add together fluctuations.

Member of exponential family of natural distributions

Epistemological reason: Maximum entropy → minimal assumptions about the data (just that the measure has finite variance)

curve( exp( -x^2 ) , from=-3 , to=3 )








Gaussian is continuous - value \(y\) can be any continuous value. In contrast to binomial, which requires integers.

Probability mass functions: discrete outcomes (like binomial) → denoted \(Pr\)

Cannot be greater than 1

Probability density functions: continuous outcomes → denoted \(P\) or \(f\) .

can be greater than 1

Probability density is the rate of change in cumulative probability
Area under the density function will never exceed 1 = probability mass












TipRecipe for statistical models




Recognize set of variables we want to understand. Data are observable variables. Parameters are unobservable, like rates and averages.
For each variable, define it either in terms of other variables or a probability distribution
Combination of variables and their probability distributions defines a joint generative model that can be used both to simulate hypothetical observations as well as analyze real ones.









NoteSummarizing the model



\(y_{i}\) ~ \(Normal(µ_{i}, σ)\)
\(µ{i} = 𝛽x{i}\)
\(𝛽\) ~ \(Normal(0,10)\)
\(σ\) ~ \(Exponential(1)\)
\(x_{i}\) ~ \(Normal(0,1)\)


Revising the globe-tossing model:
\[W \sim {\sf Binom}(N, p)\]
\[p \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,1)\]

Likelihood function used in Bayes’ thm: The count \(W\) is distributed binomially with sample size N and probability \(p\)
Define priors: The prior for \(p\) is assumed to be uniform between 0 and 1

Stochastic: indicated by ~ symbol. No single instance of the variable on left is known with certainty, but is instead characterized by a probabilistic mapping

w <- 6; n <- 9;
p_grid <- seq(0,1,length.out=100)
posterior <- dbinom(w,n,p_grid) * dunif(p_grid,0,1)
posterior <- posterior/sum(posterior)




Loaded the data, not place them into convenient object

d <- Howell1


Data frame simply named d: special kind of list in R, table with named columns, correponding with variables, and numbered rows, corresponding to individual cases


# str() compactly display the structure of an R object 
str(d)

'data.frame':   544 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ height: num  152 140 137 157 145 ...
 $ weight: num  47.8 36.5 31.9 53 41.3 ...
 $ age   : num  63 63 65 41 51 35 32 27 19 54 ...
 $ male  : int  1 0 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 ...

# precis() helpful for summarizing posterior distr further on 
precis(d)

              mean         sd      5.5%     94.5%     histogram
height 138.2635963 27.6024476 81.108550 165.73500 ▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▇▇▅▁
weight  35.6106176 14.7191782  9.360721  54.50289 ▁▂▃▂▂▂▂▅▇▇▃▂▁
age     29.3443934 20.7468882  1.000000  66.13500     ▇▅▅▃▅▂▂▁▁
male     0.4724265  0.4996986  0.000000   1.00000    ▇▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▇


Working with columns

$ → extract the column named height from the data frame d


d$height


d2 <- d[d$age >= 18,]


Index notation: [row, column]


dens(d2$height)









Height raw data looks approx Gaussian, BUT not a good idea to gawk at raw data and decide how to model them

Write general model and compute plausibility of each µ and σ. To define the heights as normally distributed with a mean µ and sd σ:
\[h_{i} \sim {Normal}(µ,σ) \]

h → list of heights
subscript i –> each individual element of list, takes on row numbers (1-32, no. heights in d2$height )

All the golem knows about each height measurement is defined by the name normal distribution with mean µ and standard dev σ. The model assumes that the values \(h_{i}\) are independent and identically distributed (IDD). In other words, each value of h has the same probability function, independent of the other h values and using the same parameters. But hardly true - heights within families are correlated.


The parameters to be estimated are µ and σ → so need prior \(Pr(µ, σ)\) or the joint prior probability for all parameters. Assume that they’re independent of each other or \(Pr(µ, σ) = Pr(µ)Pr(σ)\)
\[h_{i} \sim {Normal}(µ,σ) \]
\[µ \sim{Normal}(178, 20)\]
\[σ \sim {Uniform}(0, 50)\]
The prior for µ is a broad Gaussian prior, centered on 178cm, with 95% of probability between 178 ±40.

Why 178 cm? Author is 178 cm tall. And the range from 138 cm to 218 cm encompasses a huge range of plausible mean heights for human populations. So domain-specific information has gone into this prior. Everyone knows something about human height and can set a reasonable and vague prior of this kind.

Whatever the prior, it’s a very good idea to plot your priors, so you have a sense of the assumption they build into the model.

curve(dnorm(x,178,20), from=100, to=250, xlab = "mu",ylab="density")









the golem is assuming that the average height (not each individual height) is almost certainly between 140 cm and 220 cm.

The σ prior is a truly flat prior, a uniform one, that functions just to constrain σ to have positive probability between zero and 50cm. View it with:

curve(dunif(x,0,50), from=-10, to=60)












See what your priors imply about the distribution of heights
Helps diagnose bad choices
Simulate heights by sampling from the prior


sample_mu <- rnorm(1e4, 178,20)
sample_sigma <- runif(1e4,0,50)
prior_h <- rnorm(1e4, sample_mu, sample_sigma)
dens(prior_h, xlab="height")









Expected distribution of heights, averaged over the prior
Prior prob distribution is not itself Gaussian - not an empirical expectation but a distribution of relative plausibilities of different heights, BEFORE seeing the data

Compare to a less informative prior for average height µ ~ Normal(178,100). Priors with large SDs are common in Bayesian models, but not really sensible.

sample_mu <- rnorm(1e4, 178,100)
prior_h <- rnorm(1e4, sample_mu, sample_sigma)
dens(prior_h)
abline(v=0, lty = "dashed") #plot line at x=0 to show where negative values occur









4% of expected heights are negative. Also expects some giants: 18% of expected heights over 272cm (tallest record)





For the first time modeling Gaussian distribution, demonstrate calculations with brute force (usually impractical)

mu.list <- seq( from=150, to=160 , length.out=100 )
sigma.list <- seq( from=7 , to=9 , length.out=100 )
post <- expand.grid( mu=mu.list , sigma=sigma.list )
post$LL <- sapply( 1:nrow(post) , function(i) sum(
dnorm( d2$height , post$mu[i] , post$sigma[i] , log=TRUE ) ) )
post$prod <- post$LL + dnorm( post$mu , 178 , 20 , TRUE ) +
dunif( post$sigma , 0 , 50 , TRUE )
post$prob <- exp( post$prod - max(post$prod) )

contour_xyz(post$mu, post$sigma, post$prob)







image_xyz(post$mu, post$sigma, post$prob)









inspect the posterior distribution (in post$prob ) with functions like contour_xyz() or image_xyz() in the rethinking package




To summarize and understand the posterior distribution, like in Ch3. New thing: since 2 parameters and need to sample combos of them, we first randomly samples row numbers in post in proportion to values in post$prob. Then pull out parameter values on those randomly sampled rows.

sample.rows <- sample(1:nrow(post), size=1e4, replace=TRUE, prob=post$prob)
sample.mu <- post$mu[sample.rows]
sample.sigma <- post$sigma[sample.rows]


Output: 1e4 samples, with replacement, from the posterior for height data, plotted below:


plot(sample.mu, sample.sigma, cex=0.5, pch=16, col=col.alpha(rangi2,0.1))









col.alpha() makes the colors transparent → demonstrates density (overlapping samples)
cex (character expansion, size of points) a numerical vector giving the amount by which plotting characters and symbols should be scaled relative to the default.
pch (plot character) a vector of plotting characters or symbols

Plot the densities of µ and σ → characterizing the shapes of the marginal posterior densities of µ and σ.

Marginal: averaging over the other parameters


dens(sample.mu)







dens(sample.sigma)









PI(sample.mu)

      5%      94% 
153.9394 155.2525 

PI(sample.sigma)

      5%      94% 
7.323232 8.252525 


Since these samples are just vectors of numbers, you can compute any statistic from them that you could from ordinary data.

The linear model strategy. Make the parameter for the mean of a Gaussian distribution µ ito a linear function of the predictor variable and other new parameters we invent.

We ask the golem: “Consider all the lines that relate one variable to the other. Rank all of these lines by plausibility, given these data.”
The golem answers with a posterior distribution.

NoteChoosing priors



Priors encode states of info before seeing the data.

In cases with good prior info that discounts the plausibility of some parameter values (e.g., neg associations between height and weight) - encode directly in priors
Vary priors and repeat the analysis in order to study how different states of initial info influence inference
Often, many reasonable priors produce same inference
Conventional Bayesian priors are conservative relative to conventional non-Bayesian approaches
Choose priors conditional on pre-data knowledge of the data (constraints, ranges, theoretical relationships) never conditional on the observed sample

Briefly, B-splines divide the full range of some predictor variable (e.g., year) into parts. Then they assign a parameter to each part. These parameters are gradually turned on and off in a way that makes their sum into a fancy, wiggly curve.

Generate new predictor variables and use those in the linear model, \(µ_{i}\)
Invent series of new, synthetic predictor variables (basis functions), each of which serves to gradually turn a specific parameter on and off within a specific range of the predictor variables
Now the linear model:

\[ µ_{i} = \alpha + w_{1}B_{i,1} + w_{2}B_{i,2} + w_{3}B_{i,3} + ...\]

where \(B_{i,n}\) is the n-th basis function’s value on row \(i\) and the \(w\) parameters are corresponding weights for each. parameters act as slopes, adjusting the influence of each \(B\) on the mean \(µ_{i}\)



Simple case: Approximate temp data with 4 different linear approximations

Divide the full range of x-axis into N parts, using pivot points called knots.
At each knot, one basis function has value 1, the rest are set to 0.
At any point on the x-axis, only 2 basis functions have non-zero values, so the parameters for those two basis functions are the only parameters influencing the prediction at a given x-point (year).

Compared to polynomial regression, in which parameters influence the entire shape of the curve

Each basis function is multiplied by its corresponding (positive or negative) weight parameter, which are derived from fitting the model to the data
To improve the simple case:

Use more knots
Use higher degree polynomials instead of linear approx

Third, define the model and make it run to get the parameter weights for each basis function. Each column of matrix B as variable. Get intercept to capture the average temp - priors on base weights will be deviation from the intercept.
\[T_{i} \sim Normal(µ_{i}, σ)\]
\[µ_{i} = \alpha + \sum_{k=1}^{K}{w_{k}B_{k,i}}\]
As for the priors:
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(6,10)\]

Intercept: The mean of 6 deg Celsius is the historical average March temp in Kyoto. The SD of 10 is weakly informative - allows the intercept to span roughly -14C to 26C

\[w_{j} \sim {\sf Normal}(0,1)\]

Spline weights: Mean = 0: no knot region is expected to deviate from the intercept (baseline temp) by default. SD of 1 is regularizing, no crazy wiggles - spline can shift µi by roughly +/-1 C at any knot region

\[sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1)\]

SD: The residual year-to-year temperature variability around the spline trend. Exponential suports only positive reals = \(\sigma\) > 0. Encodes weakly informative belief that sigma is probably not enormous, with a soft tail. Rate =1 means the prior mean is 1 - gentle regularizer that nudges sigma away from 0 and from large values

quap and matrix multiplication. Make sure to use a start list for the weights to tell quap how many there are.

B %*% w is shorthand for (1) multiplying each element of the vector w by each value in the corresponding column of B and then (2) summing up each row of the result.


m4.7 <- quap(
  alist(
    T ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + B %*% w,
    a ~ dnorm(6,10),
    w ~ dnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ),
  data=list(T=d2$temp, B=B),
  start=list(w=rep(0,ncol(B)))
)

Plot the posterior predictions for 17 w functions.

# See the weighted basis functions 
post <- extract.samples(m4.7)
w <- apply(post$w, 2, mean)
plot(NULL, xlim=range(d2$year), ylim=c(-2,2), 
     xlab="year", ylab="basis * weight")
for (i in 1:ncol(B)) lines(d2$year, w[i]*B[,i])








The 97% posterior interval for µ, at each year:

mu <- link(m4.7)
mu_PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI, 0.97)
plot(d2$year, d2$temp, col=col.alpha(rangi2,0.3),pch=16)
shade(mu_PI, d2$year, col=col.alpha("black",0.5))

title: Ch 4: Geocentric Models
text:
TipRecipe for statistical models




Recognize set of variables we want to understand. Data are observable variables. Parameters are unobservable, like rates and averages.
For each variable, define it either in terms of other variables or a probability distribution
Combination of variables and their probability distributions defines a joint generative model that can be used both to simulate hypothetical observations as well as analyze real ones.









NoteSummarizing the model



\(y_{i}\) ~ \(Normal(µ_{i}, σ)\)
\(µ{i} = 𝛽x{i}\)
\(𝛽\) ~ \(Normal(0,10)\)
\(σ\) ~ \(Exponential(1)\)
\(x_{i}\) ~ \(Normal(0,1)\)


Revising the globe-tossing model:
\[W \sim {\sf Binom}(N, p)\]
\[p \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,1)\]

Likelihood function used in Bayes’ thm: The count \(W\) is distributed binomially with sample size N and probability \(p\)
Define priors: The prior for \(p\) is assumed to be uniform between 0 and 1

Stochastic: indicated by ~ symbol. No single instance of the variable on left is known with certainty, but is instead characterized by a probabilistic mapping

w <- 6; n <- 9;
p_grid <- seq(0,1,length.out=100)
posterior <- dbinom(w,n,p_grid) * dunif(p_grid,0,1)
posterior <- posterior/sum(posterior)

title: Ch 4: Geocentric Models
text:
Loaded the data, not place them into convenient object

d <- Howell1


Data frame simply named d: special kind of list in R, table with named columns, correponding with variables, and numbered rows, corresponding to individual cases


# str() compactly display the structure of an R object 
str(d)

'data.frame':   544 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ height: num  152 140 137 157 145 ...
 $ weight: num  47.8 36.5 31.9 53 41.3 ...
 $ age   : num  63 63 65 41 51 35 32 27 19 54 ...
 $ male  : int  1 0 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 ...

# precis() helpful for summarizing posterior distr further on 
precis(d)

              mean         sd      5.5%     94.5%     histogram
height 138.2635963 27.6024476 81.108550 165.73500 ▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▇▇▅▁
weight  35.6106176 14.7191782  9.360721  54.50289 ▁▂▃▂▂▂▂▅▇▇▃▂▁
age     29.3443934 20.7468882  1.000000  66.13500     ▇▅▅▃▅▂▂▁▁
male     0.4724265  0.4996986  0.000000   1.00000    ▇▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▇


Working with columns

$ → extract the column named height from the data frame d


d$height


d2 <- d[d$age >= 18,]


Index notation: [row, column]


dens(d2$height)









Height raw data looks approx Gaussian, BUT not a good idea to gawk at raw data and decide how to model them

Write general model and compute plausibility of each µ and σ. To define the heights as normally distributed with a mean µ and sd σ:
\[h_{i} \sim {Normal}(µ,σ) \]

h → list of heights
subscript i –> each individual element of list, takes on row numbers (1-32, no. heights in d2$height )

All the golem knows about each height measurement is defined by the name normal distribution with mean µ and standard dev σ. The model assumes that the values \(h_{i}\) are independent and identically distributed (IDD). In other words, each value of h has the same probability function, independent of the other h values and using the same parameters. But hardly true - heights within families are correlated.


The parameters to be estimated are µ and σ → so need prior \(Pr(µ, σ)\) or the joint prior probability for all parameters. Assume that they’re independent of each other or \(Pr(µ, σ) = Pr(µ)Pr(σ)\)
\[h_{i} \sim {Normal}(µ,σ) \]
\[µ \sim{Normal}(178, 20)\]
\[σ \sim {Uniform}(0, 50)\]
The prior for µ is a broad Gaussian prior, centered on 178cm, with 95% of probability between 178 ±40.

Why 178 cm? Author is 178 cm tall. And the range from 138 cm to 218 cm encompasses a huge range of plausible mean heights for human populations. So domain-specific information has gone into this prior. Everyone knows something about human height and can set a reasonable and vague prior of this kind.

Whatever the prior, it’s a very good idea to plot your priors, so you have a sense of the assumption they build into the model.

curve(dnorm(x,178,20), from=100, to=250, xlab = "mu",ylab="density")









the golem is assuming that the average height (not each individual height) is almost certainly between 140 cm and 220 cm.

The σ prior is a truly flat prior, a uniform one, that functions just to constrain σ to have positive probability between zero and 50cm. View it with:

curve(dunif(x,0,50), from=-10, to=60)












See what your priors imply about the distribution of heights
Helps diagnose bad choices
Simulate heights by sampling from the prior


sample_mu <- rnorm(1e4, 178,20)
sample_sigma <- runif(1e4,0,50)
prior_h <- rnorm(1e4, sample_mu, sample_sigma)
dens(prior_h, xlab="height")









Expected distribution of heights, averaged over the prior
Prior prob distribution is not itself Gaussian - not an empirical expectation but a distribution of relative plausibilities of different heights, BEFORE seeing the data

Compare to a less informative prior for average height µ ~ Normal(178,100). Priors with large SDs are common in Bayesian models, but not really sensible.

sample_mu <- rnorm(1e4, 178,100)
prior_h <- rnorm(1e4, sample_mu, sample_sigma)
dens(prior_h)
abline(v=0, lty = "dashed") #plot line at x=0 to show where negative values occur









4% of expected heights are negative. Also expects some giants: 18% of expected heights over 272cm (tallest record)





For the first time modeling Gaussian distribution, demonstrate calculations with brute force (usually impractical)

mu.list <- seq( from=150, to=160 , length.out=100 )
sigma.list <- seq( from=7 , to=9 , length.out=100 )
post <- expand.grid( mu=mu.list , sigma=sigma.list )
post$LL <- sapply( 1:nrow(post) , function(i) sum(
dnorm( d2$height , post$mu[i] , post$sigma[i] , log=TRUE ) ) )
post$prod <- post$LL + dnorm( post$mu , 178 , 20 , TRUE ) +
dunif( post$sigma , 0 , 50 , TRUE )
post$prob <- exp( post$prod - max(post$prod) )

contour_xyz(post$mu, post$sigma, post$prob)







image_xyz(post$mu, post$sigma, post$prob)









inspect the posterior distribution (in post$prob ) with functions like contour_xyz() or image_xyz() in the rethinking package




To summarize and understand the posterior distribution, like in Ch3. New thing: since 2 parameters and need to sample combos of them, we first randomly samples row numbers in post in proportion to values in post$prob. Then pull out parameter values on those randomly sampled rows.

sample.rows <- sample(1:nrow(post), size=1e4, replace=TRUE, prob=post$prob)
sample.mu <- post$mu[sample.rows]
sample.sigma <- post$sigma[sample.rows]


Output: 1e4 samples, with replacement, from the posterior for height data, plotted below:


plot(sample.mu, sample.sigma, cex=0.5, pch=16, col=col.alpha(rangi2,0.1))









col.alpha() makes the colors transparent → demonstrates density (overlapping samples)
cex (character expansion, size of points) a numerical vector giving the amount by which plotting characters and symbols should be scaled relative to the default.
pch (plot character) a vector of plotting characters or symbols

Plot the densities of µ and σ → characterizing the shapes of the marginal posterior densities of µ and σ.

Marginal: averaging over the other parameters


dens(sample.mu)







dens(sample.sigma)









PI(sample.mu)

      5%      94% 
153.9394 155.2525 

PI(sample.sigma)

      5%      94% 
7.323232 8.252525 


Since these samples are just vectors of numbers, you can compute any statistic from them that you could from ordinary data.
Sample size and the normality of the standard dev’s posterior: Posterior is not always so Gaussian in shape. For a Gaussian likelihood and a Gaussian prior on µ, the posterior distribution is always Gaussian as well, regardless of sample size. It is the standard deviation σ that causes problems. So if you care about σ—often people do not—you do need to be careful of abusing the quadratic approximation.
Posterior of σ has long right-hand tail. Variances (SDs) must be positive (more uncertainty about how big it is rather than how small it is.
Sample with small size of 20 heights:

d3 <- sample(d2$height, size=20)

# repeat code from previous subsection
mu.list <- seq( from=150, to=170 , length.out=200 )
sigma.list <- seq( from=4 , to=20 , length.out=200 )
post2 <- expand.grid( mu=mu.list , sigma=sigma.list )
post2$LL <- sapply( 1:nrow(post2) , function(i)
sum( dnorm( d3 , mean=post2$mu[i] , sd=post2$sigma[i],log=TRUE ) ) )
post2$prod <- post2$LL + dnorm( post2$mu , 178 , 20 , TRUE ) +
dunif( post2$sigma , 0 , 50 , TRUE )
post2$prob <- exp( post2$prod - max(post2$prod) )
sample2.rows <- sample( 1:nrow(post2) , size=1e4 , replace=TRUE ,
prob=post2$prob )
sample2.mu <- post2$mu[ sample2.rows ]
sample2.sigma <- post2$sigma[ sample2.rows ]
plot( sample2.mu , sample2.sigma , cex=0.5 ,
col=col.alpha(rangi2,0.1) ,
xlab="mu" , ylab="sigma" , pch=16 )








Inspect the marginal posterior density for σ, averaging over µ, produced with:

dens( sample2.sigma , norm.comp=TRUE )









the posterior for σ is not Gaussian, but rather has a long tail of uncertainty towards higher values





Quadratic approximation: quickly make inferences about the shape of the posterior. The posterior’s peak → maximum a posteriori estimate (MAP) = useful image of posterior’s shape at this peak
quap in rethinking - define the posterior probability at each combination of parameter values.

Then climbs the posterior distribution and find the peak, its MAP.
Estimates the quadratic curvature at the MAP to produce an approximation of the posterior distribution.
Remember: This procedure is very similar to what many non-Bayesian procedures do, just without any priors.


library(rethinking) # repeat code to load data and select out adults
data(Howell1)
d <- Howell1
d2 <- d[ d$age >= 18 , ]




Model definition
R code




\(h_{i} \sim {Normal}(µ,σ)\)
height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma)


\(µ \sim{Normal}(178, 20)\)
mu ~ dnorm(178,20)


\(σ \sim {Uniform}(0, 50)\)
sigma ~ dunif(0,50)




flist <- alist(
  height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
  mu ~ dnorm(178, 20),
  sigma ~ dunif(0,50)
)

Fit model to the dataframe d2:

# fit model stored in m4.1
m4.1 <- quap(flist, data=d2)

#look at posterior distribution 
precis(m4.1)

            mean        sd      5.5%      94.5%
mu    154.607031 0.4119946 153.94858 155.265478
sigma   7.731331 0.2913859   7.26564   8.197022


These numbers provide Gaussian approximations for each parameter’s marginal distribution. This means the plausibility of each value of µ, after averaging over the plausibilities of each value of σ, is given by a Gaussian distribution with mean 154.6 and standard deviation 0.4.
Start values for quap climbing a hill - needs to start at some combo of parameter values (usually random vals sampled from prior). Possible to specify starting val, like the mean and sd in this context.

start <- list(
  mu=mean(d2$height),
  sigma=sd(d2$height)
)
m4.2 <- quap(flist, data=d2, start=start)

Difference between alist and list: both make collections of arbitrary R objects

list evaluates the code embedded inside - use when defining list of start values
alist does not execute code inside

Using a more informative prior (mean of 0.1 = narrow prior). µ won’t change much, but the estimate for σ does

m4.2 <- quap(
  alist(
    height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu ~ dnorm(178,0.1),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,50)
  ), data = d2
)
precis(m4.2)

           mean        sd      5.5%     94.5%
mu    177.86375 0.1002354 177.70356 178.02395
sigma  24.51756 0.9289232  23.03297  26.00216


Sampling from quap.

A quadratic approx to a posterior distribution with more than one parameter (e.g., µ and σ) is just a multi-dimensional Gaussian distribution
quap calculates deviations for all parameters and also covariances among pairs of parameters

A list of means and a matrix of variances and covariances - sufficient to describe a multi-dimensional Gaussian distribution


Variance-Covariance Matrix: shows how each parameter relates to every other parameter in the posterior distribution.

vcov(m4.1)

                mu        sigma
mu    0.1697395234 0.0002182073
sigma 0.0002182073 0.0849057204


A variance-covariance matrix can be factored into two elements: (1) a vector of variances for the parameters and (2) a correlation matrix that tells us how changes in any parameter lead to correlated changes in the others.

diag(vcov(m4.1)) # list of variances, if squared = the SDs in precis output 

        mu      sigma 
0.16973952 0.08490572 

cov2cor(vcov(m4.1)) # correlation matrix 

               mu       sigma
mu    1.000000000 0.001817646
sigma 0.001817646 1.000000000



List of variances: if squared, we get the SDs in the precis output
Correlation matrix: correlations are close to 0, so learning µ tells us little about σ and vice versa

Sample vectors of values from a multi-dimensional Gaussian distribution. extract.samples() from the rethinking package.

extract.samples uses mvrnorm() which is like rnorm but simulates random vectors of multivariate Gaussian values.


post <- extract.samples(m4.1, n=1e4)
head(post)

        mu    sigma
1 154.4396 8.075498
2 154.7473 7.724383
3 154.8098 8.043616
4 154.5094 7.827165
5 154.1050 7.648885
6 154.3617 7.958263


You end up with a data frame, post, with 10,000 (1e4) rows and two columns, one column for µ and one for σ. Each value is a sample from the posterior

precis(post)

            mean        sd       5.5%      94.5%    histogram
mu    154.602170 0.4069462 153.955790 155.255320     ▁▁▁▅▇▂▁▁
sigma   7.730445 0.2927892   7.257834   8.199296 ▁▁▁▂▅▇▇▃▁▁▁▁

print("Vs m4.1 posterior")

[1] "Vs m4.1 posterior"

precis(m4.1)

            mean        sd      5.5%      94.5%
mu    154.607031 0.4119946 153.94858 155.265478
sigma   7.731331 0.2913859   7.26564   8.197022

#Compare o the grid approx
plot(post)

title: Ch 4: Geocentric Models
text:
Predictor variable: independent variable we posit predicts the outcome if it has statistical association with the outcome variable.
How Kalahari height (outcome var) covaries with weight (predictor var). Seems dull now because readers don’t have a theory about growth and life history in mind.
Plot the height and weight against one another to get a sense of how they covary:

plot(d2$height, d2$weight)








How to incorporate predictor vars into Gaussian model?
The linear model strategy. Make the parameter for the mean of a Gaussian distribution µ ito a linear function of the predictor variable and other new parameters we invent.

This instructs the golem to assume that the predictor variable has a constant and additive relationship to the mean of the outcome. It then computes the posterior distribution of this constant relationship







We ask the golem: “Consider all the lines that relate one variable to the other. Rank all of these lines by plausibility, given these data.”
The golem answers with a posterior distribution.



Case study: one predictor variable (weight). How to get weight into Gaussian model of height? Define µ as a function of values in x (d2$weight), with \(\overline{x}\) as the average of weights.








\(h_{i} \sim {Normal}(µ_{i},σ)\)
likelihood
height ~ dnorm(mu,sigma)




\(µ_{i} = \alpha + \beta(x_{i} - \overline x)\)
linear model
mu ← a + b*weight


\(\alpha \sim{Normal}(178, 20)\)
\(\alpha\) prior
a ~ dnorm(178, 20)


\(\beta \sim{Normal}(0,10)\)
\(\beta\) prior
b ~ dlnorm(0,1)


\(σ \sim {Uniform}(0, 50)\)
\(\sigma\) prior
sigma ~ dunif(0,50)





Probability of the observed height. The mean µ noe depends on unique values on each row i.



The mean µ is not longer a parameter to be estimated, instead \(µ_{i}\) is determined by other parameters \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), and the observed variable \(x\). We know \(µ_{i}\) with certainty (not stochastic). \(x_{i}\) is weight value on row \(i\).
Asks two questions:

What is the expected height when \(x_{i} = \overline{x}\) ? \(µ_{i} = \alpha\) when \(x_{i} = \overline{x}\).
What is the change in expected height when \(x_{i}\) changes by 1 unit? \(\beta\) is the slope - rate of change in expectation

Find the line that relates \(x\) to \(h\) - a line that passes through \(\alpha\) when \(x_{i} = \overline{x}\) and has slope \(\beta\)



These last priors define distributions for the unobserved variables.
\(\beta\) prior: why Gaussian prior with mean 0?
Simulate a hundred pairs of alpha and beta:

set.seed(2971) 
N <- 100      #100 lines
a <- rnorm(N,178,20)
b <- rnorm(N,0,10)

Now plot the lines:

plot(NULL,xlim=range(d2$weight), ylim=c(-100,400), xlab="weight", ylab="height")

abline(h=0, lty=2) # no one is negative height
abline(h=272, lty=1, lwd=0.5) # tallest person 

mtext("b ~ dnorm(0,10")
xbar <- mean(d2$weight) 
for (i in 1:N) curve(a[i] + b[i] *(x-xbar),from = min(d2$weight),to=max(d2$weight), add=TRUE, col=col.alpha("black", 0.2))









Relationship between weight and height can be absurdly positive or negative
Know that height INC with avg weight. Restrict to positive values → define prior as \(\beta \sim{Log-Normal}(0,1)\). Log of \(\beta\) has a Normal(0,1) distribution

dlnorm and rlnorm densities for working with log-normal distributions

b <- rlnorm(1e4, 0,1)
dens(b, xlim=c(0,5), adj=0.1)









If log of beta is normal, then beta itself is strictly positive

Re-doing the prior predictive simulation with Log-Normal

set.seed(2971)
N <- 100 
a <- rnorm(N, 178,20)
b <- rlnorm(N,0,1)

# plotting
plot(NULL,xlim=range(d2$weight), ylim=c(-100,400), xlab="weight", ylab="height")

abline(h=0, lty=2) # no one is negative height
abline(h=272, lty=1, lwd=0.5) # tallest person 

mtext("log(b) ~ dnorm(0,1)")
xbar <- mean(d2$weight) 
for (i in 1:N) curve(a[i] + b[i] *(x-xbar),from = min(d2$weight),to=max(d2$weight), add=TRUE, col=col.alpha("black", 0.2))









Now all lines in the joint prior for alpha and beta are within human reason

Important to fuss over priors (even if they end up being irrelevant due to big data). Because some priors may end up being relevant for many other analyses and it helps us build better models.






NoteChoosing priors



Priors encode states of info before seeing the data.

In cases with good prior info that discounts the plausibility of some parameter values (e.g., neg associations between height and weight) - encode directly in priors
Vary priors and repeat the analysis in order to study how different states of initial info influence inference
Often, many reasonable priors produce same inference
Conventional Bayesian priors are conservative relative to conventional non-Bayesian approaches
Choose priors conditional on pre-data knowledge of the data (constraints, ranges, theoretical relationships) never conditional on the observed sample






Just incorporate new model of the mean into the model specification inside quap and make sure to add a prior for the new parameter \(\beta\)

#load data again, since it's a long way back 
library(rethinking)
data("Howell1")
d <- Howell1
d2 <- d[d$age >= 18,]

# define the average weight, x-bar 
xbar <- mean(d2$weight)

#fit model 
m4.3 <- quap(
  alist(
    height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b*(weight - xbar),
    a ~ dnorm(178,20),
    b ~ dlnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,50)
  ),
  data=d2)




Tables of marginal distributions: inspect the marginal posterior distributions of the parameters

precis(m4.3)

             mean         sd        5.5%       94.5%
a     154.6013671 0.27030766 154.1693633 155.0333710
b       0.9032807 0.04192363   0.8362787   0.9702828
sigma   5.0718809 0.19115478   4.7663786   5.3773831


Focus on new parameter \(\beta\). Mean on 0.9 = a person 1kg heavier is expected to by 0.90 cm taller. 89% of the posterior probability lies between 0.84 and 0.97. \(\beta\) vals close to 0 or greatly above 1 are highly incompatible with these data and this model.

Not suggesting that the relationship between height and weight are linear, just that: if you’re committed to a line, then lines with slope 0.9 are plausible ones

Also need variance-covariance matrix to describe the quadratic posterior completely, along with precis()

round(vcov(m4.3), 3)

          a     b sigma
a     0.073 0.000 0.000
b     0.000 0.002 0.000
sigma 0.000 0.000 0.037


Very little covariation among the parameters.

pairs(m4.3) #shows both marginal posteriors and covariance 

Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter









Plotting posterior inference against the data.
Plot raw data, compute posterior mean values for a and b, draws implied line.

plot(height ~ weight, data=d2, col=rangi2)
post <- extract.samples(m4.3)
a_map <- mean(post$a)
b_map <- mean(post$b)
curve(a_map + b_map * (x - xbar), add=TRUE)








Each point in this plot is a single individual. The black line (posterior mean) is defined by the mean slope β and mean intercept α. This is not a bad line. But lots of other highly plausible lines near it.
Adding uncertainty around the mean.
Each combo of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) has posterior probability. How to get uncertainty into the plot: sample a bunch of lines from the posterior distribution, display lines on plot to visualize the uncertainty in the regression relationship
Work with all the samples from the model

post <- extract.samples(m4.3)
post[1:5,]

         a         b    sigma
1 154.5789 0.9376825 5.220756
2 154.4067 0.8937310 4.752735
3 154.4622 0.9150822 5.341227
4 154.2649 0.9236067 5.160423
5 155.1258 0.9495934 5.108891



each row is a correlated random sample from the joint posterior of all three parameters, using the covariances provided by vcov(m4.3)

The average of very many of these lines = posterior mean line
Scatter around the average alters our confidence in the relationship between the predictor and outcome


Display bunch of the lines incrementally - see scatter

N <- 100
dN <- d2[1:N,]
mN <- quap(
  alist(
    height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b*(weight - mean(weight)),
    a ~ dnorm(178,20),
    b ~ dlnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,50)
  ), data=dN
)

# Extract 20 samples from the posterior 
post <- extract.samples(mN, n=20)

# Display raw data and sample size 
plot(dN$weight, dN$height, 
     xlim=range(d2$weight), ylim=range(d2$height),
     col=rangi2, xlab="weight", ylab="height")
mtext(concat("N = ", N))

# Plot the lines, with transparency 
for (i in 1:20)
  curve(post$a[i] + post$b[i]*(x - mean(dN$weight)),
        col=col.alpha("black", 0.3), add=TRUE)









Notice that the cloud of regression lines becomes more compact as the sample size (N) increases. Model grows more confident about location of mean

Plotting regression intervals and contours: More informative to see uncertainty by plotting an interval or contour around the average regression line.
Make list of 10,000 vals of µ for an individual who weights 50kg (\(x_{i}\)) via samples from posterior
\[µ_{i} = \alpha + \beta(x_{i}-\overline{x}) \]

post <- extract.samples(m4.3)
mu_at_50 <- post$a + post$b * (50 - xbar)

# Plotting mu_at_50 = Vector of predicted means, one for each random sample from the posterior 
dens(mu_at_50, col=rangi2, lwd=2, xlab="mu|weight=50")








Since the components of µ have distributions, so too does µ. And since the distributions of α and β are Gaussian, so to is the distribution of µ (adding Gaussian distributions always produces a Gaussian distribution).
Since the posterior for µ is a distribution, you can find intervals for it, just like for any posterior distribution.

PI(mu_at_50, prob=0.89)

      5%      94% 
158.5785 159.6799 



the central 89% of the ways for the model to produce the data place the average height between about 159 cm and 160 cm (conditional on the model and data), assuming the weight is 50 kg.

That’s good so far, but we need to repeat the above calculation for every weight value on the horizontal axis, not just when it is 50 kg. Use the link function from rethinking. It takes the quap approx, samples from the posterior distribution, and computes µ for each case in the data and sample from the post distribution.

mu <- link(m4.3)
str(mu)

 num [1:1000, 1:352] 158 157 157 157 157 ...



Output: big matrix of µ values

Each row = sample from post distri (default = 1000 samples)
Each column = case in the data (352 columns in this matrix)

This is a distribution of µ for each individual in the original data

Now, let’s get a distribution of µ for each unique weight value on the horizontal axis:

# Define sequence of wights to compute predictions for 
# these values will be on the horiz axis
weight.seq <- seq(25, 70, by=1)

# Use link() to compute mu 
# For each sample from posterior 
# and for each weight in weight.seq
mu <- link(m4.3, data=data.frame(weight=weight.seq))
str(mu)

 num [1:1000, 1:46] 136 136 136 137 137 ...



Now only 46 columns in mu - fed it 46 diff values for weight

Visualize by plotting the distribution of µ values at each height

# Use type="n" to hide raw data 
plot(height ~ weight, d2, type="n")

# Loop over samples and plot each mu value 
for (i in 1:100)
  points(weight.seq, mu[i,], pch=16, col=col.alpha(rangi2,0.1))









At each weight value in weight.seq, a pile of computed µ values are shown. Each of the piles is a Gaussian distribution

The amount of uncertainty in µ depends on the value of weight


Summarize the distribution for each weight value, using apply()

# Summarize the distribution of mu 

#Compute the mean of each column (dimension "2") of the matrix mu 
mu.mean <- apply(mu, 2, mean)   #contains the average mu at each weight value

#Compute the PI (89% interval) of each column of the matrix mu 
mu.PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI, prob=0.89)   #contains 89% lower and upper bounds for each weight value 

Plot these summaries on top of the data

#plot raw data 
# fading out points to make line and interval more visible 
plot(height ~ weight, data=d2, col=col.alpha(rangi2,0.5))

# Plot the MAP line, aka the mu for each weight 
lines(weight.seq, mu.mean)

# Plot the shaded region for 89% PI 
shade(mu.PI, weight.seq)








Using this approach, can derive and plot the posterior prediction means and intervals for quite complicated models, for any data you choose.






TipRecipe for generating predictions and intervals from the posterior of a fit model




Use link to generate distributions of posterior values for µ. The default behavior of link is to use the original data, so you have to pass it a list of new horiz axis values you want to plot posterior predictions across
Use summary functions like mean or PI to find averages and lower and upper bounds of µ for each value of the predictor variable
Finally, use plotting functions like lines or shade to draw the lines and intervals. Or you might plot the distributions of the predictions, or do further numerical calculations with them

Recipe words for every model we fit in the book. As long as you know how parameters relate to the data, you can use samples from the posterior to describe any aspect of the model’s behavior.


Prediction intervals - for actual heights, not just mean heights \(h_{i} \sim {Normal}(µ_{i},σ)\)

Spread around µ govered by \(\sigma\) → need to incorporate into predictions
sim() → Simulating heights: for each unique weight value, sample from a Gaussian distribution with the correct mean µ for the weight and correct value of SD \(\sigma\) from the same posterior distribution. Simulation embodies the uncertainty in the posterior AND the Gaussian distribution of heights


sim.height <- sim(m4.3, data=list(weight=weight.seq))
str(sim.height)

 num [1:1000, 1:46] 136 131 140 139 136 ...



This matrix contains simulated heights, NOT distributions of plausible avg height, µ

Summarize the simulated heights using apply

# Assin the 89% posterior prediction interval of observable (according to the model) heights, across the values of weight in weight.seq 
height.PI <- apply(sim.height, 2, PI, prob=0.89)


# Plot raw data 
plot(height ~ weight, d2, col=col.alpha(rangi2, 0.5))

# Draw MAP line 
lines(weight.seq, mu.mean)

# Draw HPDI region for line 
mu.HPDI <- apply(mu, 2, HPDI, 0.89) # not sure about this..
shade(mu.HPDI, weight.seq)

# Draw PI region for simulated heights
shade(height.PI, weight.seq)









89% prediction interval for height as function of weight.

Solid line = average line for the mean height at each weight
Narrow shaded interval = distribution of µ
Wider shaded region = region within which the model expects to find 89% of the actual heights in the population, at each weight

Uncertainty in both the parameter values AND in the sampling process

library(rethinking)
data("cherry_blossoms")
d <- cherry_blossoms
precis(d)

Briefly, B-splines divide the full range of some predictor variable (e.g., year) into parts. Then they assign a parameter to each part. These parameters are gradually turned on and off in a way that makes their sum into a fancy, wiggly curve.

Generate new predictor variables and use those in the linear model, \(µ_{i}\)
Invent series of new, synthetic predictor variables (basis functions), each of which serves to gradually turn a specific parameter on and off within a specific range of the predictor variables
Now the linear model:

\[ µ_{i} = \alpha + w_{1}B_{i,1} + w_{2}B_{i,2} + w_{3}B_{i,3} + ...\]

where \(B_{i,n}\) is the n-th basis function’s value on row \(i\) and the \(w\) parameters are corresponding weights for each. parameters act as slopes, adjusting the influence of each \(B\) on the mean \(µ_{i}\)



Simple case: Approximate temp data with 4 different linear approximations

Divide the full range of x-axis into N parts, using pivot points called knots.
At each knot, one basis function has value 1, the rest are set to 0.
At any point on the x-axis, only 2 basis functions have non-zero values, so the parameters for those two basis functions are the only parameters influencing the prediction at a given x-point (year).

Compared to polynomial regression, in which parameters influence the entire shape of the curve

Each basis function is multiplied by its corresponding (positive or negative) weight parameter, which are derived from fitting the model to the data
To improve the simple case:

Use more knots
Use higher degree polynomials instead of linear approx





First, choose the knots (values of year to serve as pivots). In principle, you can put them wherever you like (assumptions of the model). But it’s often useful to place knots at evenly spaced quantiles of the predictor variable.

Temperature data, year variable is evenly distributed. Place 15 knots (ran again with 20)


d2 <- d[complete.cases(d$temp),] #complete cases on temp 
num_knots <- 20 #15
knot_list <- quantile(d2$year, probs=seq(0,1,length.out=num_knots))
knot_list

       0% 5.263158% 10.52632% 15.78947% 21.05263% 26.31579% 31.57895% 36.84211% 
 839.0000  916.1053  975.2105 1034.3158 1093.4211 1152.5263 1211.6316 1270.7368 
42.10526% 47.36842% 52.63158% 57.89474% 63.15789% 68.42105% 73.68421% 78.94737% 
1329.8421 1388.9474 1448.0526 1507.1579 1566.2632 1625.3684 1684.4737 1743.5789 
84.21053% 89.47368% 94.73684%      100% 
1802.6842 1861.7895 1920.8947 1980.0000 


Second, choose your polynomial degree. This determines how basis functions combine, which determines how the parameters interact to produce the spline.

Deg 1 → 2 basis functions combine
Deg 2 → 3 basis functions combine
Deg 3 → 4 basis functions combine

R has built in splines library with function bs() to construct basis functions for any list of knots, degree.

# call splines library
library(splines)

# Build basis functions for cubic (deg3) spline 
B <- bs(d2$year, 
        knots=knot_list[-c(1,num_knots)],
        degree=3, intercept=TRUE)


B is a matrix with 1124 rows (year corresponding to rows in d2 data frame) and 17 columns (basis functions).


# Display the basis functions by plotting each column against year 
plot(NULL, xlim=range(d2$year), ylim=c(0,1), xlab="year", ylab="basis value")

# for each column in matrix B, plot line(year ~ column i)
for (i in 1:ncol(B)) lines(d2$year, B[,i]) 








Third, define the model and make it run to get the parameter weights for each basis function. Each column of matrix B as variable. Get intercept to capture the average temp - priors on base weights will be deviation from the intercept.
\[T_{i} \sim Normal(µ_{i}, σ)\]
\[µ_{i} = \alpha + \sum_{k=1}^{K}{w_{k}B_{k,i}}\]
As for the priors:
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(6,10)\]

Intercept: The mean of 6 deg Celsius is the historical average March temp in Kyoto. The SD of 10 is weakly informative - allows the intercept to span roughly -14C to 26C

\[w_{j} \sim {\sf Normal}(0,1)\]

Spline weights: Mean = 0: no knot region is expected to deviate from the intercept (baseline temp) by default. SD of 1 is regularizing, no crazy wiggles - spline can shift µi by roughly +/-1 C at any knot region

\[sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1)\]

SD: The residual year-to-year temperature variability around the spline trend. Exponential suports only positive reals = \(\sigma\) > 0. Encodes weakly informative belief that sigma is probably not enormous, with a soft tail. Rate =1 means the prior mean is 1 - gentle regularizer that nudges sigma away from 0 and from large values

quap and matrix multiplication. Make sure to use a start list for the weights to tell quap how many there are.

B %*% w is shorthand for (1) multiplying each element of the vector w by each value in the corresponding column of B and then (2) summing up each row of the result.


m4.7 <- quap(
  alist(
    T ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + B %*% w,
    a ~ dnorm(6,10),
    w ~ dnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ),
  data=list(T=d2$temp, B=B),
  start=list(w=rep(0,ncol(B)))
)

Plot the posterior predictions for 17 w functions.

# See the weighted basis functions 
post <- extract.samples(m4.7)
w <- apply(post$w, 2, mean)
plot(NULL, xlim=range(d2$year), ylim=c(-2,2), 
     xlab="year", ylab="basis * weight")
for (i in 1:ncol(B)) lines(d2$year, w[i]*B[,i])








The 97% posterior interval for µ, at each year:

mu <- link(m4.7)
mu_PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI, 0.97)
plot(d2$year, d2$temp, col=col.alpha(rangi2,0.3),pch=16)
shade(mu_PI, d2$year, col=col.alpha("black",0.5))
