title: Lec 3: Geocentric Models
text:
Step 1: Question/goal/estimand

describe association between adult weight and height

title: Lec 3: Geocentric Models
text:
Step 2: Scientific model
How does height causally influence weight?

DAG:

\[H → W ← U\]
\[W = f(H, U)\]

“Weight is some function of height and unobserved stuff”


Generative models
Options

Dynamic: incremental growth of organism; both mass and height (length) derive from growth pattern; Gaussian variation result of summed fluctuations
Static: (what we’re doing) imagine association between variables w and h at particular age ranges but no mechanism, still at Gaussian variation, imagined as a result of growth history (but not modeled)

For adults, weight is a proportion of height plus the influence of unobserved causes:
\[ W = \beta H + U\]

beta is some proportion



Generative code

# function to simulate weights of individuals from height 
sim_weight <- function(H,b, sd) { 
  "simulate U using rnorm for each individual in H, using mean of 0 and sd = standard 
  deviation of U, unobserved noise"
  U <- rnorm(length(H), 0, sd) 
  W <- b*H + U
  return(W)
}


Goal - estimate \(\beta\) but right now, simulating what data look like for any given value of beta

“This is the generative model: can it produce data that looks anything like the original data?” →

H <- runif(200, min=130, max=170) # why uniform? just cuz he wanted the full x-axis represented
#H <- rnorm(200, 170,20)
#plot(H)

W <- sim_weight(H, b=0.5, sd=5)
plot(W~H, col=2, lwd=3)









Yes, it can (doesn’t mean it’s the right generative model)
Simulated individuals → biologically realistic relationships between weight and height

title: Lec 3: Geocentric Models
text:
Step 3: Statistical model(s)






NoteConventional statistical model notation



(1) List the variables
(2) Define each variable as a deterministic or distributional function of other variables









\(W_{i} = \beta H_{i} + U_{i}\)
Equation for expected weight


\(U_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(0, \sigma)\)
Gaussian error with standard deviation sigma


\(H_{i} \sim {\sf Uniform}(130,170)\)
Height uniformly distributed from 130-170cm




Estimator
We want to estimate how the avg weight changes with height
\[E(W_{i}|H_{i}) = \alpha + \beta H_{i}\]

\(E(W_{i}|H_{i})\) = average weight conditional on height

How this relates to posterior distributions:
\[Pr(\alpha,\beta,\sigma|H_{i},W_{i})=\frac{Pr(W_{i}|H_{i},\alpha,\beta,\sigma)Pr(\alpha,\beta,\sigma)}{Z}\]

\(Pr(\alpha,\beta,\sigma|H_{i},W_{i})\) → posterior probability of specific line
\(Pr(W_{i}|H_{i},\alpha,\beta,\sigma)\) → Garden of forking data
\(Pr(\alpha,\beta,\sigma)\) → prior
\(Z\) → normalizing



Quadratic approximation

Approximate the posterior distribution as a multivariate Gaussian distribution



Posterior distributions are very often multivariate Gaussian distributions if the sample is reasonably large






Caution



Quadratic approximation does almost what Maximum Likelihood Estimation (non-Bayesian) does in almost all cases.


quap tool so that students enter a list of deterministic and distributional assumptions that define a statistical model - runs it and finds the quadratic approximation of the posterior distribution

In statistical model, UNLIKE generative model, you need priors (when there’s no observations, what does the model believe?)

Conventionally: you could use flat priors
Recommended: concentrated priors, these do NOT build in the answer but in fact, build AWAY from the learning from the data intentionally .

Constrain implied observations of the model to scientifically realistic ranges




Prior predictive distribution → same as posterior predictive distributions (same animal, same golem)

Priors should express scientific knowledge, but softly

don’t want predictions that mimic our sample because we haven’t looked at our sample yet, we want boundaries that are realistic and reasonable
Often generative process in nature is different than we imagine → want stat model to see and learn about those violations
Scientific knowledge in this case: human biology…










Scientific knowledge (prior)
Constraint explanation
Prior distributions




When H = 0, W = 0 (someone with 0 height, should also weight 0 kg)
Strong constraint on alpha (intercept): should be close to 0, so give wide (soft) variance: \(Normal(0,10)\)
alpha is the expected value of weight when height=0
\(\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(0,10)\)


Weight INC (on average) with height (POSITIVE); Weight (kg) is less than height (cm) (BETWEEN ZERO AND ONE)
Constraint on slope: beta should be positive, between 0 and 1: \(Uniform(0,1)\)
Not the best choice, but for pedagogical reasons. Typically use Gaussian priors on slopes.
\(\beta \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,1)\)


Standard deviations are positive
Sigma must be positive → greater than 0, SD of 10 is variance of 100 kg and there’s not a variance of 100 kg around avg weight so must be in this range: \(Uniform(0,1)\)
\(\sigma \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,10)\)









ImportantNormal VS Uniform Distribution



Normal distributions:

Bell-shaped: data clusters around a central mean
Model natural phenomena

Uniform distributions:

Rectangular - all outcomes are equally likely across a range
Model consistent, equal probability scenarios





Perform prior predictive simulation

Draw the observable implications of these priors in the observable outcome space. I.e., make some lines


n <- 1e3 # num simulations 
a <- rnorm(n, 0,10) # draw n random alpha from prior distribution
b <- runif(n, 0,1) # draw n random beta from prior distribution

# Plot implied lines (50), set NULL plot has no points, 
plot(NULL, xlim=c(130,170), ylim=c(30,70), xlab="height (cm)", ylab="weight (kg)")
for (j in 1:50) abline(a=a[j], b=b[j], lwd=2, col=2)








This is what the golem imagines before seeing any data… a bit wild.

Constraint on beta from 0 to 1 is reasonable - so the slopes are not bad.
However, many lines are too low… impossibly so. Someone who is 170cm is not gonna be, on avg 30kg. High lines are impossibly high.

To see this prior predictive distribution (and the implications of your assumptions), as an expert in your field, in this visual way - you realize your assumptions are bad

Leave these priors for now. Won’t do damage in this simple model. Bayesian is gonna learn the proper relationships among the variables quickly right away.






NoteSermon on priors




FALSE ASSUMPTION: Bayesian stats is frequentism + priors



Priors are just posterior distributions. It’s the posterior distribution, and how it’s computed, that’s diff from frequentist stats
There are no correct priors, only scientifically justifiable priors (same with posteriors)

Scientific assumptions justify the generative model, which justify the estimator
Justify with info outside the data - like the rest of model
Priors are not so important in simple models
Very important/useful in complex models

Need to practice not: simulate, understand


Easy to do better than “flat” priors. If you don’t regularize, then you are exaggerating effect sizes.
Anti-Bayesian boomers worry priors are used to cheat, but priors nearly always used to shrink effects to zero! Bayes is conservative.

title: Lec 3: Geocentric Models
text:
Step 4: Validate model

Simulation-based validation

Bare minimum: test statistical model with simulated obs from scientific model
Golem might be broken
But regardless of what package you’re using (like quap), even working golems might not deliver what you hoped

Generative process - write it as code to generate synthetic data to show that your estimator, whatever structure it has, can work even in principle

Stronger test: Simulation-based calibration

More stringent tests, how calibrated Bayesian estimators are over full shape


When validating your model with simulations

Vary slope and make sure posterior mean tracks it
Use large sample to see that it converges to data-generating value
Same for other unknowns (parameters)


# Simulate a sample of 10 people 
set.seed(93)
H <- runif(10, 130, 170)
W <- sim_weight(H, b=0.5, sd=5) #data-generating slope will be 0.5, sd=5 or var of 25kg

# run the model to compare
library(rethinking)
m3.1 <- quap( 
  alist(        #quap takes a formula list that mirrors the stat model
    W ~ dnorm(mu, sigma), 
    mu <- a + b*H,
    a ~ dnorm(0,10),
    b ~ dunif(0,1),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
  ), data=list(W=W, H=H))

# summary 
precis(m3.1)

           mean         sd       5.5%      94.5%
a     5.1936596 9.42967203 -9.8767775 20.2640968
b     0.4858079 0.06515645  0.3816753  0.5899404
sigma 5.6393361 1.29435788  3.5707022  7.7079700



As you see in the precis: the model converges to the data-generating slope \(\beta\) we gave, as well as the standard deviation \(\sigma\)

But having trouble with the intercept \(\alpha\)

title: Lec 3: Geocentric Models
text:
Step 5: Analyze data
After tiresome rounds of model validation (takes very long with more complex models), you can take real data sample and the model will run.
Take Howell’s data and use it in your model

dat <- list(W=d2$weight, H=d2$height)
m3.2 <- quap(
  alist(
    W ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b*H,
    a ~ dnorm(0,10),
    b ~ dunif(0,1),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
  ), data=dat
)
precis(m3.2)

             mean         sd        5.5%       94.5%
a     -43.3772423 4.17137608 -50.0439069 -36.7105776
b       0.5717443 0.02695475   0.5286654   0.6148232
sigma   4.2533439 0.16179870   3.9947584   4.5119295



beta is around 0.5 yay
sigma is around 5
but intercept alpha is definitely not zero → suggests that there’s something globally nonlinear about the relationship between height and weight (cuz you can’t have negative weights)

But works for ADULT w and h
This intercept is just a weird, non-biological term that’s needed to make the line fit


Pairs plot plots the pairs of unknowns from the posterior distrib against one another

pairs(m3.2)

Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter
Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter










Diagonal: density of each unknown (a,b, sigma) → Gaussian bc that’s what quap produces
Upper right 3 cells: Posterior distributions as plotted from above for each pair

Intercept and slope are very correlated - strong covariation along tight line (how linear regressions often work)
Can’t interpret intercept and slope separately



First Law of statistical interpretation:

the parameters are not independent of one another and cannot be independently interpreted
Instead, push out posterior predictions and describe/interpret those

extract.samples creates synthetic data table of samples from the posterior distributions that adhere to the covariance structure




Posterior predictive distribution
The posterior is full of lines

# extract samples from the model of weight as a function of height for the actual Howell sample 
post <- extract.samples(m3.2)

# Plot the Howell sample, each red dot is person in Howell's dataset 
plot(d2$height, d2$weight, col=2, lwd=3, xlab="height (cm)", ylab="weight (kg)")

# Draw 20 lines randomly sampled from the posterior distributions
for (j in 1:20)
  abline(a=post$a[j], b=post$b[j], lwd=1)








Bayesian updating perspective

… more red dots - more narrow range of lines

The posterior is full of people

Lines of posterior - slopes very little bit but in a fairly narrow range

Estimates ONLY the AVERAGE relationship between weight and height

Most of red dots are not on the line → Lots of variation from the U (unobserved stuff)

Sometimes you want the U on the graph, which comes from sigma

# Plot the Howell sample, each red dot is person in Howell's dataset 
plot(d2$height, d2$weight, col=2, lwd=3, xlab="height (cm)", ylab="weight (kg)")

# Draw 20 lines randomly sampled from the posterior distributions
for (j in 1:20)
  abline(a=post$a[j], b=post$b[j], lwd=1)

# put some new data ranging between 130-190 cm
height_seq <- seq(130, 190, len=20) 

# use sim, give it the fit quap model and the new data 
W_postpred <- sim(m3.2,
                  data=list(H=height_seq))

#take percentile interval for each height value 
W_PI <- apply(W_postpred, 2, PI)
lines(height_seq, W_PI[1,], lty=2, lwd=2)
lines(height_seq, W_PI[2,], lty=2, lwd=2)

title: Lec4: Categories and Curves
text:
Now we need to block association thru H
Need to stratify by H


S <- rbern(100)+1 # simulate sample of sexes
dat <- sim_HW(S, b=c(0.5,0.5), a=c(0,10)) #different alpha, assume +10kg for men - direct effect

plot(dat$H, dat$W, col=c("red","blue")[S], xlab="height(cm)", ylab="weight (kg)")

abline(v=mean(dat$H), h=mean(dat$W), lty=3)


indirect: H influences W differently (slopes)
Direct: W differs net any slope differences




Ignore sex for a moment, regression on weight from height

\[W_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(µ_{i}, \sigma)\]
\[µ_{i} = \alpha + \beta(H_{i} - \overline{H})\]

Centering H makes it so that alpha is the average weight of a person with average height.
Centering makes it easier to define scientific priors for alpha

alpha = expected weight at the expected height

so when \(H_{i} = \overline{H}\) → \(\beta\) * 0 → beta/slope has no effect



Now let’s add sex
\[µ_{i} = \alpha_{S[i]} + \beta_{s[i]}(H_{i} - \overline{H})\]

\(S[i]\) sex of i-th person (1=female, 2=male)

\[\alpha = [\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}],  \beta = [\beta_{1},\beta_{2}]\]

Two intercepts and two slopes, one for each value in S





data("Howell1")
d <- Howell1
d <- d[d$age >= 18,]
dat <- list(
  W = d$weight,
  H = d$height,
  Hbar = mean(d$height),
  S = d$male + 1) 

m_SHW <- quap(
  alist(
    W ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a[S] + b[S]*(H-Hbar),
    a[S] ~ dnorm(60,10),
    b[S] ~ dunif(0,1),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
  ), data=dat, 
  start = list(
    a = c(60, 60),
    b = c(0.4, 0.4),
    sigma = 6)
)

Contrasts at each height

Compute posterior predictive for women
Compute posterior predictive for men
Subject (2) from (1)
Plot distribution at each height


xseq <- seq(130,190, len=50)
plot(NULL, xlim=range(xseq), ylim=c(-6,8), xlab="height (cm)", ylab="weight contrast (F - M)")


muF <- 
  link(m_SHW, data=list(S=rep(1,50), H=xseq,Hbar=mean(d$height)))
  lines(xseq, apply(muF,2,mean), lwd=3, col=2)

muM <- 
  link(m_SHW, data=list(S=rep(2,50), H=xseq,Hbar=mean(d$height)))
  lines(xseq, apply(muM,2,mean), lwd=3, col=4)

mu_contrast <- muF - muM
for (p in c(0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,0.99))
  shade(apply(mu_contrast,2,PI,prob=p), xseq)
abline(h=0, lty=2)


Posterior distribution of differences of in expected weight at each height between men and women according to the model
Gravity’s around 0, not much difference at any height between men and women’s heights

Taller women tend to weigh more than men of the same height
Shorter men tend to weigh more than women of same height

Nearly all of the causal effect of sex on weight acts thru height

The weight contrast distribution straddles zero line
Mean differences in weight by sex, but that’s because men are taller


So, almost no DIRECT effect of sex on weight in this population






NoteSummary: Category variables




Easy to use with index coding
Use samples to compute relevant contrasts
Always summarize (mean, intervals) as the last step

Do not summarize first and then take a difference

Want mean difference and NOT difference of means

title: Lec4: Categories and Curves
text:
Polynomial linear models

Strategy: polynomial functions \(µ_{i} = \alpha + \beta_{1}x_{i} + \beta_{2}x^{2}_{i}\)
Still linear because it’s an additive function of the parameters (parameters are not exponentiating anything)
Problems: strange symmetries (not a scientifically reasonable assumption), explosive uncertainty at edges

Stem from polynomials inability to smooth locally, but globally (at whole x-axis at once - any data point in any region of the x-axis can change the shape of the curve)

DO NOT USE

Thinking vs Fitting

Linear models can fit anything (Geocentrism)
Better to think: (will come back in Chapter 19)

title: Ch5: The Many Variables & the Spurious Waffles
text:
Spurious Association

# load data and copy
library(rethinking)
data("WaffleDivorce")
d <- WaffleDivorce

# standardize variables
d$A <- scale(d$MedianAgeMarriage)
d$D <- scale(d$Divorce)


# Replication of Divorce rate by Median age marriage plot 
plot(d$D ~ d$A, xlab="Median age marriage", ylab="Divorce rate")














CautionWhy Standardize?



Outcome and predictor variables are on completely different scales.
For example,

d$D Divorce rate is in divorces per 1000 people
s$A Median Age at Marriage is in years

Their raw regression coefficients aren’t directly comparable. A coefficient of 0.5 on age means something very different on divorce rate.
By standardizing both variables to have mean = 0 and SD = 1, you can now directly compare: 1 unit change in each variable means same thing - one standard deviation. This lets you answer “which predictor has a stronger relationship with the outcome?” just by comparing coefficient sizes.



Linear regression model for Divorce rate by Median Age at Marriage
\[D_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_{i},\sigma)\]
\[\mu_{i} = \alpha + \beta_{A}A_{i}\]
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.2)\]
\[\beta_{A} \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.5)\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1)\]
\(D_{i}\) is the standardized (zero-centered, SD=1) divorce rate for State \(i\), and \(A_{i}\) is State \(i\)’s standardized median age at marriage.
Priors, explained

\(\alpha\) should be close to 0 since both outcome and predictor variables are standardized.
If \(\beta_{A}\) = 1, implies a change in 1 SD in age at marriage is associated likewise with 1 SD of change in divorce.


# How big is the SD of age at marriage?
sd(d$MedianAgeMarriage)

[1] 1.24363


So when \(\beta_{A} = 1\), a change of 1.2 years in median age at marriage is associated with a full SD change in the outcome variable. Insanely strong relationship. So beta prior should be more conservative: only 5% of plausible slopes are more extreme than 1.

Compute approx posterior

m5.1 <- quap(
  alist(
    D ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bA* A,
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bA ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data = d
)



Simulate priors

set.seed(10)
prior <- extract.prior(m5.1)
mu <- link(m5.1, post=prior, data=list(A=c(-2,2)))

# plot lines over the range of 2 standard deviations for both outcome, predictor 
plot(NULL, xlim=c(-2,2), ylim=c(-2,2), xlab="Median age marriage (std)", ylab="divorce rate (std)")
for (i in 1:50) lines(c(-2,2), mu[i,], col=col.alpha("black", 0.4))










Posterior predictions

# compute percentile interval of mean 
A_seq <- seq(-3,3.2, length.out=30)
mu <- link(m5.1, data=list(A=A_seq))
mu.mean <- apply(mu, 2, mean)
mu.PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI)

# plot everything 
plot(D ~ A, data=d, col=rangi2) # raw data 
lines(A_seq, mu.mean, lwd=2)
shade(mu.PI, A_seq)







# summarize model 
precis(m5.1)

               mean         sd       5.5%      94.5%
a      1.182907e-09 0.09737878 -0.1556301  0.1556301
bA    -5.684034e-01 0.10999982 -0.7442044 -0.3926024
sigma  7.883258e-01 0.07801137  0.6636486  0.9130030


Same process for Marriage Rate and Divorce Rate

# standardize marriage rate data 
d$M <- scale(d$Marriage)

# quad approx of linear model
m5.2 <- quap(
  alist(
    D ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bM * M,
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bM ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)
precis(m5.2)

              mean         sd       5.5%     94.5%
a     2.918030e-07 0.10824642 -0.1729984 0.1729990
bM    3.500540e-01 0.12592744  0.1487977 0.5513104
sigma 9.102653e-01 0.08986239  0.7666479 1.0538828



relationship between Marriage Rate and Divorce Rate is not as strong Median Age and Divorce Rate
Only comparing parameter means between different bivariate regressions is no way to decide which predictor is better. Both of these predictors could provide independent value, or they could be redundant, or one could eliminate the value of the other.

DAGs before Regression
Is there a direct effect of marriage rate on divorce rate, or rather is age at marriage just driving both, creating a spurious correlation between marriage rate and divorce rate?

library(dagitty)
dag5.1 <- dagitty("dag{
                   A -> D
                   A -> M
                   M -> D }")
dag5.2 <- dagitty("dag{
                   A -> D
                   A -> M
                  }")

# plot out where the vars go (x plane vs y plane)
coordinates(dag5.1) <- list(x=c(A=0, D=1, M=2), y=c(A=0,D=1, M=0))
drawdag(dag5.1)







coordinates(dag5.2) <- list(x=c(A=0, D=1, M=2), y=c(A=0,D=1, M=0))
drawdag(dag5.2)








conditional independencies: model’s testable implications

statements of which vars should be associated with each other (or not) in data
statements of which vars become dis-associated when we condition on some other set of variables
formal notation:

implication that some variable Y is not associated with some var X, after conditioning on some other var Z: \(Y \mathrel{\unicode{x2AEB}} X|Z\)



# All variables are correlated with one another
cor(d$D, d$A)

           [,1]
[1,] -0.5972392

cor(d$D,d$M)

          [,1]
[1,] 0.3737314


Testable Implications

First DAG:

Testable implication: all pairs of vars should be associated, whatever we condition on.




Second DAG: M has no influence on D, but they are still correlated with one another, because A influences them both (same cause)

Once we condition on A, nothing more we can learn thru M
Testable implication: All pairs of vars are associated, before conditioning on anything; D is independent of M, conditional on A: \(D \mathrel{\unicode{x2AEB}} M|A\)



# dagitty can find conditional indepencies for you 

# Check for cond. indepen. for dag2
DMA_dag2 <- dagitty('dag{D <- A -> M}')
impliedConditionalIndependencies(DMA_dag2)

D _||_ M | A



# Check for cond. indepen. for dag1
DMA_dag1 <- dagitty('dag{ D <- A -> M -> D }')
impliedConditionalIndependencies(DMA_dag1)

# diplays no output (=no conditional independencies)

Once you fit a multiple regression to predict divorce using both marriage rate and age at marriage, the model addresses the questions

After I already know marriage rate, what additional value is there in also knowing age at marriage?
After I already know age at marriage, what additional value is there in also knowing marriage rate?

The answer to these q’s = parameter estimates, which are descriptive results

text:
Multiple Regression






NoteMultiple Regression Formula Strategy




Nominate the predictor variables you want in the linear model of the mean
For each predictor, make a parameter that will measure its association with the outcome
Multiply the parameter by the variable and add that term to the linear model



\[D_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_{i},\sigma)\]
\[\mu_{i} = \alpha + \beta_{M}M_{i} + \beta_{A}A_{i}\]
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.2)\]
\[\beta_{M} \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.5)\]
\[\beta_{A} \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.5)\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1)\]
Multiple Linear Regression Model

Expected outcome for any State (i) with Marriage Rate (Mi) and Median Age at Marriage (Ai) is the sum of 3 independent terms: \(\alpha\), the product \(M_{i} * \beta_{M}\) (association between Marriage Rate and Divorce Rate), and the product \(A_{i} * \beta_{i}\) (association between Median Age at Marriage and Divorce)
\(+\) symbols read as “or” - A state’s divorce rate can be a function of its marriage rate or its median age at marriage.. = independent associations (may be purely statistical or rather causal)


Compute approx posterior

m5.3 <- quap(
  alist(
    D ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + (bM * M) + (bA*A),
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2), 
    bM ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    bA ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data = d
)
precis(m5.3)

               mean         sd       5.5%      94.5%
a     -2.828642e-05 0.09707123 -0.1551669  0.1551103
bM    -6.553086e-02 0.15076312 -0.3064794  0.1754177
bA    -6.136370e-01 0.15097351 -0.8549218 -0.3723521
sigma  7.850672e-01 0.07783076  0.6606786  0.9094558



Compare Models
Visualize posterior distributions for all 3 models with focus on slope parameters \(\beta\)’s. Plot the coefficient table with the coeftab() function, which allows you to compare the posterior means (circles) and 89% compatibility intervals (solid lines)

plot(coeftab(m5.1,m5.2, m5.3), par=c("bA","bM"))









bA doesn’t move, only grows a little uncertain, while bM is only associated with the divorce when Median Age is missing from the model (i.e., when using model m5.2)
So:

Once we know median age at marriage for a State, there is little or no additional predictive power in also knowing the rate of marriage in that State.

This tests the implication of the second DAG from earlier. Since the first DAG did not imply this result, it is out.

Implies no direct causal path from marriage to divorce rate: the association between marriage rate and divorce rate is spurious, caused by the influence of age of marriage on both marriage rate and divorce rate

cor(d$A, d$M)

text:
Plot multivariate predictors
Visual plots to help understand inferences from MLR models.. Three interpretive plot examples:

Interpretive Plots for MLR







Plot example
What they show
What they’re good for




Predictor residual plots
How outcome against residual predictor values
Understanding the statistical model, not much else

When predictor variables are additively related to each other


Posterior prediction plots
Model-based predictions against raw data or otherwise display error in prediction
Checking fit and assessing predictions
NOT causal tools


Counterfactual plots
Implied predictions for imaginary experiments.
Explore the causal implications of manipulating one or more variables




Predictor residual plots

predictor variable residual: average prediction error when using all other predictor variables to use a predictor of interest
In order to compute residuals for two predictors (Marriage Rate M, and Median Age A), use the other predictor to model one predictor

\[M_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_{i},\sigma)\]
\[\mu_{i} = \alpha + \beta_{A}A_{i}\]
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.2)\]
\[\beta \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.5)\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1)\]

Priors: since we standardized both vars, expect the mean \(\alpha\) to be around 0 → reuse priors


# Code approx posterior 
m5.4 <- quap(
  alist(
    M ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bAM * A,
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bAM ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)


Compute the residuals by subtracting the observed marriage rate in each State from the predicted rate, based on the model above


mu <- link(m5.4)
mu_mean <- apply(mu,2,mean)
mu_resid <- d$M - mu_mean

#Plot the relationship between Marriage Rate and Median Age
plot(d$M ~d$A, xlab = "Median Age at Marriage (std)",
     ylab = "Marriage Rate (std)")

# Draw predictor line 
lines(d$A, mu_mean)

# Draw vertical residual lines for each point
for (i in 1:nrow(d)) {
  lines(c(d$A[i], d$A[i]), c(d$M[i], mu_mean[i]), col = "salmon")
}









# Package residuals into a list for quap 
dat <- list(
  D = d$D,
  M_resid = mu_resid
)

# Fit a linear regression of divorce on the residuals
m5.4a <- quap(
  alist(
    D ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + b * M_resid,
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    b ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=dat
)

# Get posterior predictions over a sequence of residual values 
resid_seq <- seq(min(mu_resid), max(mu_resid), length.out=100)
mu2 <- link(m5.4a, data=list(M_resid=resid_seq))
mu2_mean <- apply(mu2, 2, mean)
mu2_PI <- apply(mu2, 2, PI)

# Plot residuals against outcome of interest, Divorce rate 
plot(mu_resid, d$D, xlab="Marriage rate residuals", ylab = "Divorce rate (STD)")

# Regression line and interval 
lines(resid_seq, mu2_mean)
shade(mu2_PI, resid_seq)

# line at 0
abline(v=0, lty=2)









Shows linear relationship between divorce and marriage rates, having statistically “controlled” for median age of marriage

Vertical line = marriage rate matches the expectation for median age at marriage

States to right of line have higher marriage rates than expected, while states to the left of line have lower marriage rates

Average divorce rates on both sides of line about the same (shown by regression line with little relationship between divorce and marriage)


If we use M to predict A and get the residuals to predict D. Then we see a relationship that states in which people marry older than expected for a given rate of marriage tend to have less divorce.






NoteWhat’s the point of predictor residual plots?



Conceptual value in seeing model-based predictions displayed against the outcome, after subtracting out influence of the other predictors.

In computing the predictor residual plots, you had to perform those calculations yourself. In the unified multivariate model, it all happens automatically. Nevertheless, it is useful to keep this fact in mind, because regressions can behave in surprising ways as a result.
Linear regression models do all of this simultaneous measurement with a very specific additive model of how the variables relate to one another. But predictor variables can be related to one another in non-additive ways. The basic logic of statistical control does not change in those cases, but the details definitely do, and these residual plots cease to be useful.




Posterior prediction plots
Checking the model’s implied predictions against the observed data.

Did the model correctly approximate the posterior distribution?
How does the model fail? - might not be a useful model for our purposes though it fits correctly

Simple posterior predictive check in the divorce example. Start by simulating predictions, averaging over the posterior

# Call link without specifying new data 
# so that it uses the original data 

mu <- link(m5.3)

# Summarize samples across cases 
mu_mean <- apply(mu,2,mean)
mu_PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI)

# Simulate observations, again no new data, so uses original data 
D_sim <- sim(m5.3, n=1e4)
D_PI <- apply(D_sim, 2, PI)

#Plot predictions against the observed data 
plot(mu_mean ~ d$D, col=rangi2, ylim=range(mu_PI), xlab="Observed divorce", ylab="Predicted divorce")

# Plot a line to show perfect prediction, intercept at 0 and slope of 1
abline(a=0, b=1, lty=2)

# Plot line segments for the confidence interval of each predictions
for (i in 1:nrow(d)) lines(rep(d$D[i],2), mu_PI[,i], col=rangi2)









The model under-predicts for States with HIGH (greater than 0) divorce rates, while it over-predicts for States with very low divorce rater (less than -1)

This is norm, this is what regression does (skeptic of extreme values, so expects regression to mean)



# Label the States that frustrate the model 
# identify(x=d$D, y=mu_mean, labels=d$Loc)


What is unusual about Idaho and Utah? Both of these States have large proportions of members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Members of this church have low rates of divorce, wherever they live. This suggests that having a finer view on the demo- graphic composition of each State, beyond just median age at marriage, would help a lot to refine our understanding.



Counterfactual plots
Inferential plots that display the implied predictions of the model. They can be produced for any values of the predictor variables, even unobserved or impossible combos (like very high median age of marriage or very high marriage rate)

Helps you understand the model and generate predictions for imaginary interventions

Simplest method: holding values of all predictors except one constant. Cons: ignores the assumed causal structure (an extraordinary and evil degree of control over people would be necessary to really hold marriage rate constant while forcing everyone to marry at a later age).
How to generate plots of model predictions that take the causal structure into account:

Pick a variable to manipulate, the intervention variable.
Define the range of values to set the intervention variable to
For each value of the intervention variable, and for each sample in posterior, use the causal model to simulate the values of the other variables, including the outcome

To estimate the influence of A on M, all we need is to regress A on M, there are no other variables in the DAG creating an association between A and M. We can just add this regression to the quap() model, running two regressions at the same time:

data(WaffleDivorce)
d <- list()
d$A <- standardize( WaffleDivorce$MedianAgeMarriage )
d$D <- standardize( WaffleDivorce$Divorce )
d$M <- standardize( WaffleDivorce$Marriage )

m5.3_A <- quap(
  alist(
  ## A -> D <- M 
    D ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bM * M + bA * A,
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bM ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    bA ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1),
  # A -> M 
    M ~ dnorm(mu_M, sigma_M),
    mu_M <- aM + bAM * A,
    aM ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bAM ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma_M ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)
precis(m5.3_A)

                 mean         sd       5.5%      94.5%
a       -4.322054e-06 0.09707600 -0.1551505  0.1551419
bM      -6.537406e-02 0.15077307 -0.3063385  0.1755904
bA      -6.135131e-01 0.15098353 -0.8548139 -0.3722122
sigma    7.851176e-01 0.07784330  0.6607090  0.9095263
aM      -2.009139e-07 0.08684770 -0.1387996  0.1387992
bAM     -6.947364e-01 0.09572676 -0.8477262 -0.5417465
sigma_M  6.817355e-01 0.06757973  0.5737301  0.7897410



M and A are strongly negatively correlated. Indicates that manipulating A reduces M.


# define a range of values for A 
A_seq <- seq(-2,2, length.out=30)


par(mfrow=c(1,2))

# Prep data 
sim_dat <- data.frame(A=A_seq)

# simulate M and then D, using A_seq
s <- sim(m5.3_A, data=sim_dat, vars=c("M", "D"))

# Plot the counterfactual predictions
plot(sim_dat$A, colMeans(s$D), ylim=c(-2,2), type="l",xlab="manipulated A", ylab="counterfactual D")
shade(apply(s$D,2,PI), sim_dat$A)
mtext("Total counterfactual effect of A on D")


# simulate M using A_seq
s_M <- sim(m5.3_A, data=sim_dat, vars="M")

# Plot the counterfactual predictions
plot(sim_dat$A, colMeans(s_M), ylim=c(-2,2), type="l",xlab="manipulated A", ylab="counterfactual M")
shade(apply(s_M,2,PI), sim_dat$A)
mtext("Total counterfactual effect of A -> M")









dag5.3 <- dagitty("dag{
                   A -> D
                   M -> D }")

# plot out where the vars go (x plane vs y plane)
coordinates(dag5.3) <- list(x=c(A=0, D=1, M=2), y=c(A=0,D=1, M=0))
drawdag(dag5.3)








Now, manipulate M and keep other vars constant.

A → M is deleted bc if we control the values of M, then A no longer influences it


sim_dat <- data.frame(M=seq(-2,2,length.out=30), A=0)
s <- sim(m5.3_A, data=sim_dat, vars="D")

plot(sim_dat$M, colMeans(s), ylim=c(-2,2), type="l", xlab ="manipulated M", ylab ="counterfactual D")
shade(apply(s,2,PI), sim_dat$M)
mtext("Total counterfactual effect of M on D")









Trend is naturally less strong, since we alr fund that there is no evidence for strong influence of M on D



sim() step-by-step


# Assume we fit model m5.3_A including A -> D, and A -> M -> D
# Define a range of values to assign to A
A_seq <- seq(-2,2,length.out=30)

# extract posterior samples 
post <- extract.samples(m5.3_A)

# Simulate vals for M
M_sim <- with(post, sapply(1:30, function(i) rnorm(1e3, aM + bAM*A_seq[i], sigma_M)))
      # with() function saves us from having to type post$ in front of every parameter name

# Now simulate values for D 
D_sim <- with(post, sapply(1:30, function(i) rnorm(1e3, aM + bAM*A_seq[i] + bM*M_sim[,i],sigma)))

# Plot
plot(A_seq, apply(D_sim, 2, mean), ylim=c(-2,2), type="l",xlab="manipulated A", ylab="counterfactual D")
shade(apply(D_sim,2,PI), A_seq)
mtext("Total counterfactual effect of A on D")

text:
Masked Relationship
Another reason to use multiple predictor variables: measure the direct influences of multiple factors on an outcome, when none of those influences is apparent from bivariate relationships. This kind of problem tends to arise when there are two predictor variables that are correlated with one another. However, one of these is positively correlated with the outcome and the other is negatively correlated with it.

library(rethinking)
data(milk)
d <- milk 
str(d)

'data.frame':   29 obs. of  8 variables:
 $ clade         : Factor w/ 4 levels "Ape","New World Monkey",..: 4 4 4 4 4 2 2 2 2 2 ...
 $ species       : Factor w/ 29 levels "A palliata","Alouatta seniculus",..: 11 8 9 10 16 2 1 6 28 27 ...
 $ kcal.per.g    : num  0.49 0.51 0.46 0.48 0.6 0.47 0.56 0.89 0.91 0.92 ...
 $ perc.fat      : num  16.6 19.3 14.1 14.9 27.3 ...
 $ perc.protein  : num  15.4 16.9 16.9 13.2 19.5 ...
 $ perc.lactose  : num  68 63.8 69 71.9 53.2 ...
 $ mass          : num  1.95 2.09 2.51 1.62 2.19 5.25 5.37 2.51 0.71 0.68 ...
 $ neocortex.perc: num  55.2 NA NA NA NA ...


Popular hypothesis: primates with larger brains produce more energetic milk (for growing baby brains)
Consider variables:

kcal.per.g: Kilocalories of energy per gram of milk
mass: average female body mass, in kg
neocortex.perc: percent of total brain mass that is neocortex mass

Question: to what extent energy content of milk (in kcal) is related to neocortex %.

Standardize Variables

# standardize the three vars to get reliable approx of posterior & build reasonable priors
d$K <- scale(d$kcal.per.g)
d$N <- scale(d$neocortex.perc)
d$M <- scale(log(d$mass))



Statistical Model
First model to consider → simple bivariate regression between kcal and neocortex percent.
\[K_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(µ_{i},\sigma)\]
\[\mu_{i}= \alpha + \beta_{N}N_{i}\]

# Try to run this as quap model with vague priors, eg dnorm(0,1)
"m5.5_draft <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bN * N,
    a ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bN ~ dnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)"

This particular error message means that the model didn’t return a valid probability for even the starting parameter values. In this case, the culprit is the missing values in the N variable.


d$neocortex.perc

[13] 60.32    NA    NA 69.97    NA 70.41    NA 73.40    NA 67.53    NA 71.26

Complete Case Analysis

Complete case analysis: process to drop all the cases with missing values
complete.cases() to take only the complete cases


# Make a new data frame with only complete cases
dcc <- d[complete.cases(d$K, d$N, d$M), ]

Now, use the dcc data frame to try out quap

m5.5_draft <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bN * N,
    a ~ dnorm(0,1),
    bN ~ dnorm(0,1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=dcc
)
precis(m5.5_draft)

            mean        sd       5.5%     94.5%
a     0.09319614 0.2352206 -0.2827318 0.4691241
bN    0.15677729 0.2420543 -0.2300722 0.5436268
sigma 0.99780914 0.1640697  0.7355940 1.2600243





Simulate Priors

# Simulate and plot 50 prior regression lines
prior <- extract.prior(m5.5_draft)
xseq <- c(-2,2) # limits of standardized values for x-axis (neocortex %)

mu <- link(m5.5_draft, post=prior, data=list(N=xseq))

plot(NULL, xlim=xseq, ylim=xseq, xlab="neocortex percent (std)", ylab="kcal per g (std)")

for (i in 1:50) lines(xseq, mu[i,], col=col.alpha("black",0.3))









Tinker Priors
Crazy lines. Can do better with the priors:

With two standardized variables, when predictor is zero, the expected value of the outcome should also be zero (expected mean corresponds with expected mean). So tighter \(\alpha\) prior
The slope \(\beta_{N}\) should be tighter as well, so that it doesn’t regularly produce strong relationships


m5.5 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bN* N, 
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bN ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=dcc
)


# Plot new prior regression line simulations
prior <- extract.prior(m5.5)
mu <- link(m5.5, post=prior, data=list(N=xseq))

plot(NULL, xlim=xseq, ylim=xseq, xlab="neocortex percent (std)", ylab="kcal per g (std)")

for (i in 1:50) lines(xseq, mu[i,], col=col.alpha("black",0.3))









Still vague priors, but the lines at least stay within the high probability region of the observable data




Posterior approximation
Now look at the posterior

# summarize model
precis(m5.5)

            mean        sd       5.5%     94.5%
a     0.03993011 0.1544970 -0.2069859 0.2868461
bN    0.13319997 0.2237649 -0.2244195 0.4908195
sigma 0.99991888 0.1647479  0.7366198 1.2632179



Neither strong, nor precise association. SD is twice the posterior mean. Let’s draw a picture.

Plot the predicted mean and 89% compatibility interval for the mean

xseq <- seq(from=min(dcc$N)-0.15, to=max(dcc$N)+0.15, length.out=30)
mu <- link(m5.5, data=list(N=xseq))
mu_mean <- apply(mu, 2, mean)
mu_PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI)

plot(K ~ N, data=dcc)
lines(xseq, mu_mean, lwd=2)
shade(mu_PI, xseq)









Posterior mean line is weakly positive, but highly imprecise. A lot of mildly positive and negative slopes are plausible, given this model and these data.



Another Model: Body Mass
Now consider adult female body mass (mass). Use log(mass) as predictor as well, because often scaling measurements like body mass are related by magnitudes to other variables. Taking the log of a measure translated the measure into magnitudes.

Taking log of mass: “we suspect that the magnitude of a mother’s body is related to milk energy, in a linear fashion.”

Construct a similar model, but now consider the bivariate relationship between kilocalories and body mass.

m5.6 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bM*M,
    a ~ dnorm(0, 0.2),
    bM ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=dcc )
precis(m5.6)

             mean        sd       5.5%      94.5%
a      0.04654155 0.1512800 -0.1952331 0.28831620
bM    -0.28253565 0.1928817 -0.5907979 0.02572657
sigma  0.94927887 0.1570613  0.6982646 1.20029318



Looks like a stronger relationship, negative. Still the CIs are large enough to support positive and negative relationships


xseq <- seq(from=min(dcc$M), to=max(dcc$M), length.out=30)

mu <- link(m5.6, data=list(M=xseq))
mu_mean <- apply(mu, 2, mean)
mu_PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI)

plot(K ~ M, data=dcc, col="blue")
lines(xseq, mu_mean, lwd=2)
shade(mu_PI, xseq)










Multivariate model
Bring the predictor variables together in the same regression model

m5.7 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bN * N + bM * M,
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bN ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    bM ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=dcc
)
precis(m5.7)

             mean        sd       5.5%      94.5%
a      0.06799172 0.1339987 -0.1461641  0.2821475
bN     0.67511777 0.2482986  0.2782886  1.0719469
bM    -0.70299080 0.2207870 -1.0558511 -0.3501305
sigma  0.73801433 0.1324618  0.5263147  0.9497139


Visually compare this posterior with the previous two models:

plot(coeftab(m5.5, m5.6, m5.7), pars=c("bM", "bN"))









By incorporating both variables in the regression, the posterior association of both with the outcome has INC.

posterior mean for the association of neocortex has INC 5x
posterior mean for the log body mass has INC 2.5x

Two variables are correlated with the outcome, but one is positively correlated with it and the other is negatively correlated with it. + both of the explanatory variables are positively correlated with one another. So they tend to cancel each other out.


pairs( ~K + M + N, dcc)








Regression model asks if species that have high neocortex percent for their body mass have higher milk energy.


Simulating a masking relationship (simulate synthetic data)
Markov equivalence set: set of DAGs with the same conditional independences

# M -> K <- N 
# M -> N
n <- 100
M <- rnorm(n) # M is exogenous, nothing causes it in the DAG
N <- rnorm(n, M) # N's mean is M, so N = M+noise M->N. higher M tends to prod higher N
K <- rnorm(n, N-M) # N->K positive effect, M->K neg effect 

d_sim <- data.frame(K=K, N=N, M=M)







Note



M → N, M and N are positively correlated.
If you regress k on…

M alone: positive effect on N (which helps K) and its negative effect on K cancel out → coeff near zero
N alone: positive effect on K is partially attributed to M’s influence on N → coeff attenuated

Neither variable looks important in a bivariate model. But in the multivariate model with both M and N, the model can separate the two paths and both coeff become apparent.



# M -> K <- N 
# N -> M 
n <- 100 
N <- rnorm(n)
M <- rnorm(n, N)
K <- rnorm(n, N-M)
d_sim2 <- data.frame(K=K,N=N,M=M)

# M -> K <- N 
# M <- U -> N 
n <-100
U <- rnorm(n)
N <- rnorm(n,U)
M <- rnorm(n,U)
K <- rnorm(n, N-M)
d_sim3 <- data.frame(K=K, N=N, M=M)


May be that the positive assoc between large body size and neocortex arises arise from tradeoff between lifespan and learning. Large animals tend to live a long time. In such animals, investment in learning may be a better investment, because learning can be amortized over a longer lifespn. Both large body size and large neocortex then influence milk composition, but in different directions, for diff reasons.

This story implies DAG with M→N (first one) is more accurate (but cannot ascertain with the evidence at hand).


To compute the complete Markov equivalence set, define first DAG

dag5.7 <- dagitty("dag{
                  M -> K <- N
                  M -> N }" )
coordinates(dag5.7) <- list(x=c(M=0, K=1, N=2), y=c(M=0.5, K=1, N=0.5))
MElist <- equivalentDAGs(dag5.7)
drawdag(MElist)









While the data alone cannot tell you which causal model is correct, scientific knowledge of the variables will eliminate a large number of silly, but Markov equivalent, DAGS

Make counterfactual plots that vary one predictor while holding the others constant. In real world, these counterfactual experiments would be impossible (changing animal size → natural selection would change other features to match it). But these plots help to see how the model views the association between each predictor and outcome.

par(mfrow=c(1,2))

# Plot counterfactual holding M=0
xseq <- seq(from=min(dcc$N)-0.15, to=max(dcc$N)+0.15, length.out=30)
mu <- link(m5.7, data=data.frame(N=xseq,M=0)) # keep N constant?
mu_mean <- apply(mu,2,mean)
mu_PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI)

plot(NULL, xlim=range(dcc$M), ylim=range(dcc$K), xlab="neocortex % (std)", ylab = "kilocal per g (std)" )
lines(xseq, mu_mean, lwd=2)
shade(mu_PI, xseq)


# Plot counterfactual holding N=0
xseq <- seq(from=min(dcc$M)-0.15, to=max(dcc$M)+0.15, length.out=30)
mu <- link(m5.7, data=data.frame(M=xseq,N=0)) # keep N constant?
mu_mean <- apply(mu,2,mean)
mu_PI <- apply(mu, 2, PI)

plot(NULL, xlim=range(dcc$M), ylim=range(dcc$K), xlab="log body mass (std)", ylab = "kilocal per g (std)" )
lines(xseq, mu_mean, lwd=2)
shade(mu_PI, xseq)

title: Ch5: The Many Variables & the Spurious Waffles
text:
Categorical Variables
Categorical variables (or factors): discrete and unordered

Examples: taxonomic groups, sex, developmental status, geographic region


Binary categories

data("Howell1")
d <- Howell1
str(d)

'data.frame':   544 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ height: num  152 140 137 157 145 ...
 $ weight: num  47.8 36.5 31.9 53 41.3 ...
 $ age   : num  63 63 65 41 51 35 32 27 19 54 ...
 $ male  : int  1 0 0 1 0 1 0 1 0 1 ...


New predictor: male variable

indicator variable (dummy variable): devices for encoding unordered categories into quantitative models
male: 1
female: 0

Two approaches
(1) Indicator variable directly inside the linear model. Mathematical definition of the model, ignore other variables, just focus on sex:
\[h_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_{i}, \sigma)\]
\[\mu_{i} = \alpha + \beta_{m}m_{i}\]
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(178,20)\]
\[\beta_m \sim {\sf Normal}(0,10)\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,50) \]

\(m\) is the dummy variable indicating a male individual. \(b_m\) influences prediction only when \(m_i\) = 1. When \(m_i\) = 0, the linear model is \(\mu_i = \alpha\)

\(\beta_m\) represents the expected DIFFERENCE between males and females in height
\(\alpha\) represents the average female height (not the avg height of sample anymore)


Simulate prior distributions fo µ for females and males

mu_female <- rnorm(1e4, 178,20)
mu_male <- rnorm(1e4, 178,20) + rnorm(1e4, 0, 10)
precis(data.frame(mu_female, mu_male))

              mean       sd     5.5%    94.5% histogram
mu_female 178.1517 19.98823 146.5848 210.2721  ▁▁▃▇▇▂▁▁
mu_male   178.6922 22.39497 142.7304 214.2422 ▁▁▁▃▇▇▃▁▁



More uncertainty for “male” because prediction for male includes 2 parameters, thus, 2 priors. The priors for males is wider. But we aren’t actually more unsure about male height than female height, a priori.

(2) Index Variable: contains integers that correspond to different categories. The integers are just names, but let us reference a list of corresponding parameters

d$sex <- ifelse(d$male==1, 2, 1)
str(d$sex)

 num [1:544] 2 1 1 2 1 2 1 2 1 2 ...



Now “1” means female, and “2” means male. No order implied.

Mathematical model becomes
\[h_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_{i}, \sigma)\]
\[\mu_{i} = \alpha_{\sf SEX[i]}\]
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(178,20)   , for j = 1..2\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,50)\]

Creates a list of \(\alpha\) parameters, for each unique value in the index variables

Here, end up with two \(\alpha\) parameters, \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\)

Now, the same prior can be assigned to each member of category - corresponds to the categories are the same prior to the data

Works great in contexts with more than two categories


Approximate posterior with index variable model

m5.8 <- quap(
  alist(
    height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma), 
    mu <- a[sex],
    a[sex] ~ dnorm(178,20),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,50)
  ), data =d
)
precis(m5.8, depth = 2) # depth tells it to show any vector parameters 

           mean        sd      5.5%     94.5%
a[1]  134.91006 1.6069505 132.34185 137.47828
a[2]  142.57788 1.6974875 139.86497 145.29079
sigma  27.31022 0.8280616  25.98681  28.63362


What is the expected difference between females and males. Extract the posterior samples into a data frame and insert calculation into the same frame:

post <- extract.samples(m5.8)
post$diff_fm <- post$a[,1] - post$a[,2]
precis(post, depth=2)

              mean       sd      5.5%      94.5%       histogram
sigma    27.304361 0.832807  25.95903  28.622353       ▁▁▁▅▇▃▁▁▁
a[1]    134.913851 1.613977 132.37323 137.569285   ▁▁▁▁▂▅▇▇▅▂▁▁▁
a[2]    142.574636 1.699533 139.86233 145.319222 ▁▁▁▁▁▃▇▇▇▃▂▁▁▁▁
diff_fm  -7.660785 2.333036 -11.38003  -3.942322      ▁▁▁▃▇▇▃▁▁▁



Bottom: expected diff between a female and male in the sample
This kind of calculation is called a contrast. No matter how many categories you have, you can compute the contrast between any two by using samples from the posterior to compute their difference. Then you get the posterior distribution of the difference.



Many categories
Better to use the Index Variable approach. Does not change when you add more categories.
Back to the primate milk data, now interested in the clade variable (taxonomic membership of each species).

data(milk)
d <- milk 
unique(d$clade)

[1] Strepsirrhine    New World Monkey Old World Monkey Ape             
Levels: Ape New World Monkey Old World Monkey Strepsirrhine


Index value for each of the four categories. By hand or by coercing the factor into an integer

d$clade_id <- as.integer(d$clade)

Mathematical model
\[K_i \sim {\sf Normal}(µ_i, \sigma)\]
\[\mu_i = \alpha_{{\sf CLADE}[i]}\]
\[\alpha_j \sim {\sf Normal}(0,0.5), {\sf for} j = 1..4\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Exponential}(1)\]

widened the prior of alpha a little to allow the diff clades to disperse, if the data wants them to. But I encourage you to play with that prior and repeatedly re-approximate the posterior so you can see how the posterior differences among the categories depend upon it.


d$K <- scale(d$kcal.per.g)
m5.9 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a[clade_id],
    a[clade_id] ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)
labels <- paste("a[", 1:4, "]:", levels(d$clade), sep="")
plot(precis(m5.9, depth=2, pars="a"), labels=labels, xlab="expected kcal (std)")














Caution



used the optional labels argument to augment the parameter names a[1] through a[4]with the clade names from the original variable. In practice, you have to be very careful to keep track of which index values go with which categories. Don’t trust R’s factor variable type to necessarily do things right.


Let’s randomly assign these primates to some made up categories: [1] Gryffindor, [2] Hufflepuff, [3] Ravenclaw, and [4] Slytherin.

set.seed(63)
d$house <- sample(rep(1:4, each=8), size=nrow(d))
d$house

 [1] 1 2 3 1 3 2 1 3 4 1 4 3 3 3 1 4 4 4 2 1 1 2 3 2 3 2 1 2 4


Now include these categories as another predictor in the model

m5.10 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a[clade_id] + h[house],
    a[clade_id] ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    h[house] ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data = d
)
precis(m5.10, depth=2)

            mean         sd        5.5%        94.5%
a[1]  -0.4205602 0.26035044 -0.83665051 -0.004469931
a[2]   0.3836799 0.25968056 -0.03133976  0.798699616
a[3]   0.5664583 0.28903284  0.10452803  1.028388637
a[4]  -0.5055426 0.29664574 -0.97963974 -0.031445367
h[1]  -0.1025749 0.26170883 -0.52083620  0.315686313
h[2]  -0.1997060 0.27544061 -0.63991325  0.240501338
h[3]  -0.1603286 0.26905491 -0.59033029  0.269673120
h[4]   0.4866417 0.28751296  0.02714046  0.946142955
sigma  0.6631313 0.08812531  0.52229006  0.803972596



Slytherin stands out







WarningDifferences and Statistical Significance



One core mistake: people look at 2 parameters and reason that, for example…

\(\beta_f\) is significant (far from zero)
\(\beta_m\) is not significant (overlaps with zero)
Therefore, \(\beta_f\) and \(\beta_m\) are diff from each other.

But, this does not follow. Significance is a statement about distance from zero, not about distance from each other.
For example, suppose you have posterior distributions for two parameters,

\(\beta_f = 0.15 \pm 0.02\) → tight, clearly above 0
\(\beta_m = 0.2 \pm 0.10\) → wide, overlaps with 0 heavily

When computing the actual difference \(\beta_f - \beta_m\)

mean: 0.15 - 0.2 = 0.13
SD: \(\sqrt{0.02^2 + 0.10^2} \approx 0.10\)

So the difference is \(0.13 \pm 0.10\) which overlaps with 0 substantially. Can’t confidently claim that the two slopes differ, even though one is “significant” and the other isn’t. \(\beta_m\) is uncertain, NOT zero. The uncertainty carries forward into the comparison.
Why this happens structurally

“Not significant” means we don’t know where this parameter is — it’s compatible with zero but also compatible with values far from zero. Its distribution is wide. When you subtract a wide distribution from a narrow one, you get a wide result. The uncertainty of βm dominates the comparison.

The deeper mistake:
When βm isn’t significant, researchers often just declare it zero: “we found no effect of M.” But failing to distinguish from zero is not the same as being zero. This is accepting the null hypothesis, which classical significance testing explicitly cannot do. It only ever rejects or fails to reject. In Bayesian terms: a wide posterior centered near zero still assigns probability mass to moderate effects. Collapsing that to zero throws away real uncertainty.


If you want to know whether two parameters differ, compute the contrast directly: subtract one posterior from the other and examine that distribution. Don’t compare their individual significance statuses.

title: Ch7: Ulysses’ Compass
text:
library(rethinking)







NoteChapter Overview



Overfitting as a universal phenomenon by which models with more parameters fit a sample better, even when additional parameters are meaningless. Two tools to overcome overfitting problems: regularizing priors and estimate of out-of-sample accuracy (WAIC and PSIS).
Regularizing priors reduce overfitting during estimation, and WAIC and PSIS help estimate the degree of overfitting.
Practical functions compare help analyze collections of models fit to the same data.
If after causal estimates, then these tools will mislead. Models must be designed through some other method, not selected on the basis of out-of-sample predictive accuracy. But any causal estimate will still overfit the sample. So you always have to worry about overfitting, measuring it with WAIC /PSIS and reducing it with regularization.








TipTerms




overfitting

occurs when a model learns too much from the sample (having too many parameters), and leads to poor prediction

underfitting

placeholder

information theory

placeholder

information

the reduction of uncertainty when we learn an outcome

information entropy

the uncertainty contained in a probability distribution is the average log-probability of an event

Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence

the additional uncertainty induced by using probabilities from one distribution to describe another distribution

log-probability

logarithm of standard probability value

log-pointwise-predictive-density

Bayesian version of log-probability score; used to evaluate and compare the out-of-sample predictive accuracy of statistical models; measures how well a model predicts new data by summing the logarithm of the predictive probability of each data point.

deviance

measure of a model’s predictive inaccuracy; -2 * maximum log-likelihood of a fitted model
Indicated how well a model fits the observed data, with lower deviance being better fit

regularizing priors

skeptical prior to reduce overfitting while still allowing the model to learn sample’s regular features. Represents prior beliefs that model parameters should be smaller or closer to 0 but rarely exactly 0.

cross-validation

Splitting the train data into k folds to fit model with some folds and testing it on others to avoid overfitting
Used to estimate out-of-sample predictive accuracy via testing the model’s predictive accuracy on a small part of the sample

leave-one-out cross-validation

model evaluation technique where model is trained on all by one observation and tested on single left-out observation. Repeats for every single observation.
Overall performance calculated by averaging error scores across all observations

Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS) leave-one-out cross-validation

Highly efficient method of estimating out-of-sample predictive accuracy of model by bypassing the refitting process of leave-one-out cross-validation. via importance sampling (where the weight of an observation depends on its larger impact on the posterior distribution).

information criteria

Statistical metric used to compare models by constructing a theoretical estimate of the relative out-of-sample K-L Divergence

Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC)

Information criterion more general than AIC or DIC, making no assumption about the shape of the posterior. Provides an approximation of the out-of-sample deviance that converges to the cross-validation approximation in a large sample. Target is to guess the K-L Divergence
Lower values of WAIC indicate better performance

effective number of parameters (“overfitting penalty”)

penalty term that measures the model’s complexity; quantifies how much the model’s parameters adapt to the training data, correcting for overfitting

model comparison

analyzing multiple models to understand (1) how different variables influence predictions and (2) in combination with a causal model, implied conditional independencies among variables help us infer causal relationships

robust regression

linear model in which the influence of extreme observations is reduced

Student-t distribution

thicker-tailed distribution that arises from a mixture of Gaussian distributions with different variances.
Can be used to replace Gaussian distribution in order to reduce outlier influence in model estimation




Ockham’s Razor: the model with fewer assumptions is to be preferred

Doesn’t tell us how to navigate the tradeoff between simplicity and accuracy

Better tool: Ulysses’ compass

Scylla = Overfitting, which leads to poor prediction by learning too much from the data
Charybdis = Underfitting, which leads to poor prediction by learning too little from the data
Third monster = confounding (produce good predictions but can lead to faulty causal inferences)


Need to decide what we want from the model: do we want to understand causes OR to just predict

Two families of approaches to navigate

Regularizing prior: tell model not to get too excited about the data
Information Criteria or Cross Validation: model the prediction task and estimate predictive accuracy


Both used in social sciences, get used to both families

Information Theory
The Problem with Parameters

We shouldn’t just add more variables to our models (even when we only care about predictions, rather than causal inferences)
Adding variables (making the model more complex) always improves the fit of the data (i.e., how well a model can retrodict the data used to fit the model)
Measure of fit example: \(R^2\) “variance explained”

easy to compute
\(R^2\) INC as predictor variables are added (even random numbers)

Complex models often predict new data worse

overfit: sensitive to the exact sample used to fit it → large mistakes when future data is not exactly like past data

Simple models (too few parameters) tend to underfit, systematically over-predicting or under-predicting the data, regardless of how well future data resemble the past data






irrregular features of the data mislead, cannot generalize


sppnames <- c("afarensis","africanus","habilis","boisei",
"rudolfensis","ergaster","sapiens")
brainvolcc <- c(438 , 452 , 612, 521, 752, 871, 1350)
masskg <- c(37.0 , 35.5 , 34.5 , 41.5 , 55.5 , 61.0 , 53.5)

d <- data.frame(species=sppnames, brain=brainvolcc, mass=masskg)

Usual for brain size to correlate with body size across species. Question: to what extent do particular species have brains that are larger than expected, after taking body size into account.
Statistical control strategy:

Fit linear regression that models brain size as a function of body size (or the log of these variables for exponential relationship)
Then the remaining variation in brain size is modeled as a function of other variables, like ecology or diet

Trying our multiple models that vary in complexity…
Model 1: Linear model

Rescale the variables to get the model to fit and to understand priors

Standardize body mass (give it mean 0 and SD of 1) and rescale the outcome so that the largest observed value is 1
Don’t standardize brain size - cannot have negative brain



d$mass_std <- (d$mass - mean(d$mass))/sd(d$mass)
d$brain_std <- d$brain / max(d$brain)

\[b_i \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma)\]
\[\mu_i = \alpha + \beta m_i\]
\[\alpha \sim {\sf Normal}(0.5, 1)\]
\[\beta \sim {\sf Normal}(0,10)\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Log-Normal}(0,1)\]
Average brain volume \(b_i\) of species \(i\) is a linear function of its body mass \(m_i\)
Priors implications

\(\alpha\) prior: centered on the mean of the brain volume (rescaled) in the data. The average species with average body mass has brain volume with an 89% credible interval from about−1 to 2.

Ridiculously wide and impossible values

\(\beta\) prior: very flat centered on zero - allows absurdly large positive and negative slopes

Part of the lesson, continue on with absurd priors

m7.1 <- quap(
  alist(
    brain_std ~ dnorm(mu, exp(log_sigma)),
    mu <- a + b*mass_std,
    a ~ dnorm(0.5,1),
    b ~ dnorm(0,10),
    log_sigma ~ dnorm(0,1)
  ), data=d
)


set.seed(12)
s <- sim(m7.1)
r <- apply(s, 2, mean) - d$brain_std
resid_var <- var2(r)
outcome_var <- var2(d$brain_std)
1 - resid_var / outcome_var

title: Ch7: Ulysses’ Compass
text:
Entropy and accuracy
To navigate between underfitting/overfitting, you need to pick a criterion of model performance (target).

Establish measurement scale for distance from perfect accuracy

Info theory provides natural measurement scale for distance between two probability distributions

Establish deviance as an approximation of relative distance from perfect accuracy
Establish that only deviance out-of-sample is of interest

Defining the target (no universally best target)
Two major dimensions to worry about:

Cost-benefit analysis: how much does it cost when we’re wrong, how much do we win when we’re right?
Accuracy in context: some prediction tasks are inherently easier than others. Even if ignoring cost/benefit, still need to judge “accuracy” that accounts for how much a model could possibly improve prediction







Note



Two weather forecasters:

Original: One makes graded predictions (chance of rain on certain days: 1 1 1 0.6 0.6 0.6)
Newcomer: One makes blanket predictions (chance of rain constant across all days: 0, 0, 0, 0,…,0)

For the coarse of the 10 days (rains 3 days, sunny 7), the overall “hit rate” is higher for the newcomer.
But there are additional costs to these predictions. Audience will want to know when to bring an umbrella or not: happiness will decrease significantly if they get drenched in rain (-5 pts happiness), and decrease only slightly for the mild inconvenience of carrying an umbrella on a sunny day (-1).
So if we take the cost under consideration: the original forecaster nets \(3 \times (-1) + 7 \times (-0.6) = -7.2\) happiness. But the newcomer nets \(3 \times (-5) =-15\) happiness. So the original forecast is better.
Accuracy is different from hit rate. How to define accuracy? If we define accuracy as predicting the exact sequence of days, this means computing the probability of a correct prediction for each day, then multiplying them together to get the joint probability of correctly predicting the observed sequence.

This is the definition of accuracy that is maximized by the correct Bayesian model

So the probability for the original forecaster is \(1^3 \times 0.4^7 \approx 0.005\), while the newcomer’s is \(0^3 \times 1^7 = 0\) (has 0 probability of getting the sequence correct since they never expect rain).
Newcomer has higher average probability of being correct, terrible joint prob of being correct.
So true data-generating model will have highest joint probability. Also called the log scoring rule because typically the logarithm of the joint probability is reported.
“True” probabilities = right probabilities given our state of ignorance (which is described by the model). Probability is IN THE MODEL, not in the world.


Use log probability of the data to score the accuracy of competing models.

How to measure distance from perfect prediction

Information Theory provides solution as to how to measure the distance of a model’s accuracy from a target
Asks how much is our uncertainty reduced by learning an outcome?

EX: Forecasts issued in advance when weather is uncertain. When actual day arrives, weather is no longer uncertain. The reduction in uncertainty = measure of how much we have learned (how much information we derived from observing the outcome)
Develop precise definigiont of uncertainty → provide baseline measure of how hard it is to predict + how much improvement is possible



Information

The measured decrease in uncertainty when we learn an outcome


How to develop a principled way to quantify uncertainty (inherent in probability distribution)

EX, 2 possible weather events on particular day - either sunny or rainy (occur with some prob adding up to 1)
Function that uses the probabilities of outcomes and produces a measure of uncertainty

Many ways to measure uncertainty. Most common way to start with naming some properties a measure of uncertainty should possess:

Should be continuous
Should increase as the number of possible events increases
Should be additive

i.e., if we first measure the uncertainty of rain or shine (2 possible events) and then the uncertainty of hot or cold (2 diff possible events), the uncertainty over the 4 combos - rain/hot, rain/cold, shine/hot, shine/cold - should be the sum of the separate uncertainties



Information Entropy

If there are \(n\) different possible events and each event \(i\) has a probability \(p_i\), and we call the list of probabilities \(p\), then the unique measure of uncertainty we seek is:
\[H(p) = - E\;{\sf log}(p_i) = - \sum^n_{i-1}p_i\;{\sf log}(p_i) \]
The uncertainty contained in a probability distribution is the average log-probability of an event.

“Event” - particular type of weather, bird species, nucleotide in DNA sequence
Example with the weather forecast -
(1) Probabilities of rain (p_1 = 0.3) and shine (p_2 = 0.7)

p <- c(0.3, 0.7)
-sum(p*log(p))

[1] 0.6108643


(2) Now consider Death Valley where p_1 = 0.01 and p_2 = 0.99.

p <- c(0.01, 0.99)
-sum(p*log(p))  

[1] 0.05600153



Much lower uncertainty because it hardly rains in Death Valley → much less uncertainty about any given day

(3) Now, consider snow. Probabilities of sun, rain, and snow are p_1 = 0.7, p_2 = 0.15, and p_3 = 0.15, respectively

p <- c(0.7, 0.15, p=0.15)
-sum(p*log(p))  

[1] 0.8188085



Uncertainty/entropy tends to increase, due to the added dimensionality of the prediction problem







NoteEntropy equation details



Multiplying the average log-probability by−1 just makes the entropy H increase from zero, rather than decrease from zero. It’s conventional, but not functional.
The logarithms above are natural logs (base e), but changing the base rescales without any effect on inference. Binary logarithms, base 2, are just as common. As long as all of the entropies you compare use the same base, you’ll be fine.
The only trick in computing H is to deal with the inevitable question of what to do when p_i = 0. The log(0) = −∞, which won’t do. However, L’Hôpital’s rule tells us that \(lim_{p_i → 0} →p_i log(p_i) = 0\). So just assume that 0 log(0) = 0, when you compute H. In other words, events that never happen drop out. Just remember that when an event never happens, there’s no point in keeping it in the model.


\(H\) provides a way to quantify uncertainty → a precise way to measure how hard it is to hit the target



How to use entropy to measure how far the model is from the target

KL-Divergence

KL-Divergence

the additional uncertainty induced by using probabilities from one distribution to describe another distribution
The average difference in log probability between the target (p) and model (q)


Example: true distribution of events is p_1 = 0.3, p_2 = 0.7. If we believe instead that these events happen with probabilities q_1 = 0.25, q_2 = 0.75, how much additional uncertainty have we introduced, as a consequence of using q= {q_1, q_2} to approximate p= {p_1, p_2}?
\[D_{KL} = \sum_ip_i({\sf log}(p_i)-{\sf log}(q_i)) = \sum_i p_i{\sf log}(\frac{p_i}{ q_i}) \]
Divergence → the difference between two entropies: the entropy of the target distribution \(p\) and the cross entropy arising from using \(q\) to predict \(p\). When \(p=q\) we know the actual probabilities of the events:
\[D_{KL}(p,q) = D_{KL}(p,p) = \sum_ip_i({\sf log}(p_i)-{\sf log}(p_i)) = 0 \]
As q grows more different from p, the divergence \(D_{KL}\) also grows.
As an approximating function \(q\) becomes more accurate, \(D_{KL}(p, q)\) will shrink.

Candidate distribution that minimizes the KL divergence = closest to target







NoteCross entropy and directionality



Events arise according to actual probability, p, but are expected according to the \(q\) probabilities distributions, so the entropy is inflated, depending on how diff p and q are.

Divergence defined as additional entropy induced by using q.

Directionality matters: H(p,q) ≠ H(q,p)

Example: using Earth’s water:land ratio {0.7,0.3} to predict Mar’s ratio {0.01, 0.99} gives us KL divergence of 1.14. But if we use Mars’ ratio to predict Earth’s, then the divergence is 2.62.

Going from Mars → Earth: Mars has so little water, we’d be super surprised when we most likely land on water on Earth.
Going from Earth → Mars: Earth has good amounts of both water and land, won’t be nearly as surprised when we inevitably land on dry land on Mars, since 30% of Earth is land.







How to estimate divergence
Having identified the right measure of distance, we now need a way to estimate it in real statistical modeling tasks.
But \(p\) is unknown! That’s okay, though, because we’re only interested in the different divergences of diff candidates, say \(q\) and \(r\). Most cases, \(p\) just subtracts out because \(E{\sf log}(p_i)\) term is in both \(q\) and \(r\) divergences - no effect on the distance between q and r (and which is closer to the target \(p\)).
Compare average log-probability from each model to get estimate of the relative distance of each model from target.

Absolute magnitude is not interpretable. Only the difference \(E\log (q_i)−E\log (r_i)\) informs us about the divergence of each model from the target p

Convention to sum over all the observations \(i\), to yield a total score for model \(q\)
\[S(q) = \sum_i{\sf log} (q_i)\]

This log-probability score is gold standard to compare the predictive accuracy of different models

Estimate of \(E \; log(q_i)\) but without the final step of dividing by the number of observations



log-pointwise-predictive-density
Computing this core:

Use entire probability distribution

Since the parameters have distributions, the predictions also have a distribution

How? Find the log of the average probability for each observation \(i\), where the average is taken over the posterior distribution

Use function lppd or log-pointwise-predictive-density for the calculation on quap models



set.seed(1)
lppd(m7.1, n=1e4)

[1]  0.6098668  0.6483438  0.5496093  0.6234934  0.4648143  0.4347605 -0.8444632



Each of the values: log-probability score for a specific observation (7 observations in those data)
Summing the values → total log-probability score for the model and data

Larger values are better = larger average accuracy

Deviance: like lppd score, but multiplied by -2 (smaller values are better)




Scoring the right data

log-probability has same problem as \(R^2\) - always improves as model gets more complex

measure of retrodictive accuracy, not predictive accuracy



set.seed(1)
sapply(list(m7.1, m7.2, m7.3,m7.4,m7.5,m7.6), function(m) sum(lppd(m)))

[1]  2.490390  2.566165  3.695911  5.333750 14.109226 39.448020


Still using the training data though (used to fit the model, parameters estimated) - now need to use those estimates for new sample, the test sample.






Note




Suppose training set of size N
Compute posterior distribution of a model for the training sample, and compute the score on the training sample. Call this score \(D_{train}\)
Suppose another sample of size N from the same process, this is the test sample
Compute the score on the test sample, using the posterior trained on the training sample. Call this new score \(D_{test}\)

kseq <- 1:5 
dev <- sapply(kseq, function(k){
