title: Ch7: Ulysses’ Compass
text:
Regularization, or Golem Training

Use skeptical prior to prevent model from getting over-excited about the training sample

skeptical prior: prior that slows the rate of learning from the same

Regularizing prior: most common type of skeptical prior that reduces overfitting while still allowing the model to learn the regular features of the sample

Consider this Gaussian model







$ y_i {Normal}(_i, ) $



\(\mu_i = \alpha + \beta x_i\)
Assume predictor \(x\) is standardized so that its SD is 1 and mean 0.


$ {Normal}(0,100)$
Then prior \(\alpha\) is nearly flat prior that has no practical effect on inference


\(\beta \sim {\sf Normal}(0,1)\)
Prior on \(\beta\) is narrower, meant to regularize. This prior means that, before seeing the data, the machine should be skeptical of values above 2 and below -2 (a Gaussian prior with SD of 1 assigns only 5% plausibility to values above and below 2 SDs.
Interpretation: a change of 1 SD in \(x\) is very unlikely to produce 2 units of change in the outcome


\(\sigma \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,10)\)




Centering the prior on zero is conservative. But the narrower the prior, the more skeptical of parameter values far from zero.

Narrow: \({\sf Normal}(0,1)\)
Narrower: \({\sf Normal}(0,0.5)\)
Narrowest: \({\sf Normal}(0,0.2)\) → Most skeptical prior here

The strength of the skepticism depends on the data and model
Tuning: If too skeptical - prevent model from learning from data. Need a way to tune them.

Cross-validation: common technique to reduce overfitting by splitting data into “train” and “test” samples, then trying different priors and select the one that provides the smallest deviance from test samples

Need a lot of data

Also want a way to predict a model’s out-of-sample deviance, to forecast its predictive accuracy, using only the sample we have.







Note



Multilevel models as adaptive regularization

central device = learn the strength of the prior from the data itself

Ridge regression: linear models with slope parameters that use Gaussian priors centered at 0

takes as input a precision \(\lambda\) that describes the narrowness of the prior.

\(\lambda >0\) reduces overfitting
If \(\lambda\) is too big, then risk underfitting





Predicting predictive accuracy
Evaluate models without out-of-sample with cross-validation and info criteria. These try to guess how well models will perform, on average, in predicting new data. Both produce extremely similar approximations.

Cross-validation

Dvide sample in a number of “folds” (chunks). Model is asked to predict each fold, after training on all the others. Then, average over the score for each fold to get estimate of out-of-sample accuracy.

Minimum number of folds: 2
Other extreme: could make each point observation a folk and fit as many models as you have individual observations

cv_quap to perform cross-validation on quap models

How many folds is best?

Common advice is that both too few and too many folds produce less reliable approximations of out-of-sample performance

However, not always the case

Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV): use the maximum number of folds, resulting in leaving out one unique observation in each fold

default in cv_quap

Approximate cross-validation score without actually running the model over and over again

Use the “importance” (weight) of each observation to the posterior distribution

weight: some observations have larger impact on the posterior distribution (if we remove an important observation, the posterior changes more)
key intuition: An observation that is relatively unlikely is more important than one that is relatively expected.



Pareto-smoothed importance sampling cross-validation (PSIS): uses importance sampling (uses the importance weights approach to approximate cross-validation score)

Pareto-smoothing technique makes importance weights more reliable
Uses the Pareto distribution to derive a more reliable cross-validation score without actually doing any cross-validation
Also provides feedback about its own reliability by noting particular observations with very high weights that could make the PSIS score inaccurate



Information Criteria

Constructs a theoretical estimate of the relative out-of-sample K-L Divergence
The distance between train and test pairs (with flat priors) is approx twice the number of parameters in each model

For ordinary linear regressions with flat priors, the expected overfitting penalty is about twice the number of parameters
Phenomenon behind information criteria










Col1
Col2
Col3




Akaike Information Criteria (AIC)
Simple estimate of average out-of-sample deviance
\[AIC = D_{train}+ 2p = -2{\sf lppd}+2p\]
\(p\) = number of free parameters in posterior distribution
The dimensionality of the posterior distribution is a natural measure of the model’s overfitting tendency. More complex models tend to overfit more, directly in proportion to number of parameters
Only reliable when:

Priors are flat or overwhelmed by the likelihood
The posterior distribution is approx multivariate Gaussian
Sample size \(N\) is much greater than the number of parameters



Deviance Information Criterion (DIC)

More general than AIC
Okay with informative priors, but still assumes that the posterior is multivariate and that \(N >>k\)


Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC)
$WAIC(y,) = -2({lppd} - ivar* p (y_i|)) $
where \(y\) is the observations and \(Θ\) is the posterior distribution
More general than AIC or DIC
Makes no assumption about the shape of the posterior. Provides an approximation of the out-of-sample deviance that converges to the cross-validation approximation in a LARGE sample.
Can disagree in a finite sample because of its different target (K-L Divergence)



Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC): the log-posterior-predictive density (lppd) plus a penalty proportional to the variance in the posterior predictions
\[WAIC(y,\Theta) = -2({\sf lppd} - \sum_ivar_\theta {\sf log} p (y_i|\theta)) \]

Penalty term is the sum: means “compute the variance in log-probabilities for each observation \(i\), and then sum up these variances to get the total penalty.”

Each observation has own penalty score. Since these scores measure overfitting risk, you can assess overfitting risk at the level of each observation
also called Effective number of parameters \(p_{WAIC}\) BUT is a misleading label (less to do with number than with relations among parameters)
Call it “the overfitting penalty”
WAIC in rethinking package - computes WAIC for a model fit with quap or ulam or rstan

Like PSIS, WAIC is pointwise. Prediction is considered case by case, or point-by-point, in the data

Useful since some observations are much harder to predict than others and may also have different uncertainty
Pro: provides a (very) approximate estimate of the standard error of our estimate of out-of-sample deviance

for this SE, calculate WAIC for each observation and then exploit the central limit theorem to provide a measure of the standard error:
\[s_{\sf WAIC} = \sqrt{(N{\sf var} - 2 (lppd_i - p_i)}\]

Where \(N\) is the number of observations, \(p_i\) is the penalty term for only observation \(i\)











Caution



The validity of All these strategies to guess out-of-sample accuracy depends on the predictive task we have in mind. Not all predictions can reasonably take the form that we’ve been assuming for the train-test simulations.
For example, time series models - each prediction depends on the previous observation (which is a predictor variable for the next observation) Not easy to think of each observation as independent of/exchangeable with the others








NoteWAIC Calculations



Consider simple regression fit with quap

data(cars)
m <- quap(
  alist(
    dist ~ dnorm(mu,sigma),
    mu <- a + b*speed,
    a ~ dnorm(0,100),
    b ~ dnorm(0,10),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ) , data=cars )
set.seed(94)
post <- extract.samples(m,n=1000)

Log-likelihood of each observation i at each sample s from the posterior

n_samples <- 1000
logprob <- sapply( 1:n_samples ,
                   function(s) {
                     mu <- post$a[s] + post$b[s]*cars$speed
                     dnorm( cars$dist , mu , post$sigma[s] , log=TRUE )
                   } )


Now we have a 50x1000 matrix of log-likelihoods, with observations in rows and samples in columns.

Compute lppd, the Bayesian deviance,by averaging the samples in each row, take the log and add all the logs together

Need to do all of the averaging on the log scale with the log_sum_exp function, which computes the log of a sum of exponentiated terms. Just subtract the log of the number of samples.

This computes the average log

n_cases <- nrow(cars)
lppd <- sapply( 1:n_cases , function(i) log_sum_exp(logprob[i,]) - log(n_samples) )


Typing sum(lppd) will give the lppd.

Now, compute the penalty term, \(p_{WAIC}\) → variance across samples for each observation, added together

pWAIC <- sapply( 1:n_cases , function(i) var(logprob[i,]) )

And sum(pWAIC) returns the penalty term.
Compute WAIC:

-2*( sum(lppd) - sum(pWAIC) )

[1] 423.3309


Compare the output of the WAIC function. There will be simulation variance, because of how the samples are drawn from the quap fit. But that variance remains much smaller than the standard error of WAIC itself. Compute the standard error by computing the square root of number of cases multiplied by the variance over the individual observation terms in WAIC:

waic_vec <- -2*(lppd - pWAIC)
sqrt(n_cases * var(waic_vec))

[1] 17.83012







Comparing CV, PSIS, and WAIC

WAIC is unsurprisingly a little better at predicting out-of-sample deviance, because that is what it aims to predict.
Cross-validation (CV) is a trick that estimates out-of-sample deviance as the sample size increases, but it doesn’t aim for the right target at small sample sizes. And since PSIS approximates CV, it has the same issue.
All three do a very good job on average, and all three have the same error.
PSIS and WAIC perform very similarly in context of ordinary linear models

differences are with other model types, where the posterior distributions are not approx Gaussian or in the presence of observations that strongly influence the posterior

CV and PSIS have higher variance as estimators of the K-L Divergence, so we should expect WAIC be better in many cases
PSIS has distinct advantage in warning the user when it’s unreliable (despite slight disadvantage in accuracy)

The k values that PSIS computes for each observation indicate when the PSIS score may be unreliable, as well as identify which observations are at fault

The distance between models is what’s useful, not the absolute value of the deviance

title: Ch7: Ulysses’ Compass
text:
Model Comparison
Need to evaluate models out-of-sample (not just by looking at fit to the sample - which favors more and more complex models)
Common to perform model selection: choosing the model with the lowest criterion value and then discarding the others

DO NOT DO MODEL SELECTION (discards the information about relative model accuracy contained in the differences among the CV/PSIS/WAIC value)

Criteria purpose: measure expected predictive value of the variable on the right scale, accounting for overfitting; provide a way to measure the overfitting tendency of a model, helping us to design models and understand how statistical inference works.
Model comparison: more general approach that uses multiple models to understand both how different variables influence predictions, and in combo with a causal model, implied conditional independencies among variables help us infer causal relationships.
Two examples

About the distinction between comparing models for predictive performance vs for inferring causation
About the pointwise nature of model comparison and what inspecting individual points can reveal about model performance and mis-specification; introducing more robust alternative to Gaussian regression


Ex 1: Model Mis-selection
Inferring cause and making predictions are different tasks. CV and WAIC aim to find models that make good predictions - don’t solve any causal inference problem.

Highly confounded models can still make good predictions (at least in short-term). Backdoor paths give us valid info about statistical associations in the data. Can improve prediction, as long as we don’t intervene on system, and the future is like the past.

But since our working def of knowing a cause is that we can predict the consequences of an intervention - a good PSIS or WAIC score does not generally indicate a good causal model


Back to the plant growth and fungus example from Ch 6.

m6.6 model with just intercept
m6.7 model with both treatment and fungus (post-treatment variable)
m6.8 model that includes treatment but not fungus → the one that allowed us to correctly infer the causal influence of treatment


set.seed(71)
N <- 100 

# simulate initial heights 
h0 <- rnorm(N,10,2)

# assign treatments and simulate fungus & growth
treatment <- rep(0:1, each=N/2)
fungus <- rbinom(N,size=1, prob=0.5 - treatment*0.4)
h1 <- h0 + rnorm(N,5 - 3*fungus)

# compose a clean data frame 
d <- data.frame(h0=h0, h1=h1, treatment=treatment, fungus=fungus)

m6.6 <- quap(
  alist(
    h1 ~ dnorm( mu , sigma ),
    mu <- h0*p,
    p ~ dlnorm( 0 , 0.25 ),
    sigma ~ dexp( 1 )
  ), data=d )
m6.7 <- quap(
  alist(
    h1 ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- h0*p,
    p <- a + bt*treatment + bf*fungus,
    a ~ dlnorm(0,0.2),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    bf ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)
m6.8 <- quap(
  alist(
    h1 ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- h0*p,
    p <- a + bt*treatment,
    a ~ dlnorm(0,0.2),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)


set.seed(11)
WAIC(m6.7)

lppd

To easily compare multiple models, use convenience function compare from rethinking:

m6.7 361.9879 14.35614  0.00000       NA 3.888398 1.000000e+00
m6.8 402.8100 11.34305 40.82209 10.49435 2.662957 1.366454e-09
m6.6 405.9378 11.72436 43.94992 12.24690 1.593079 2.860200e-10



Column 1: WAIC values

Smaller values are better
Models ordered by best WAIC to worst

Model including the fungus variable has smallest WAIC, as promised


Column 2: pWAIC, penalty term of WAIC

These values are close to, but slightly below the number of dimensions in the posterior of each model, which is expected in lineaer regressions with regularizing priors

Column 3: dWAIC, difference between each model’s WAIC and best WAIC in set

0 for best model
m6.7 is about 40 units of deviance smaller than both other models
intercept model m6.6 is 3 units worse than m6.8
Are these big differences or small differences? → Are the models easily distinguished by their expected out-of-sample accuracy?

need to consider error in WAIC estimates


Columns 4: SE, standard error of each WAIC

expect out-of-sample accuracy to be normally distributed with mean equal to the reported WAIC value and SD equal to the standard error

Column 5: dSE, standard error of the models’ difference

each difference in WAIC values has a standard error
To compute the standard error of the difference between models m6.7 and m6.8, we just need the pointwise breakdown of the WAIC values:

set.seed(91)
waic_m6.7 <- WAIC( m6.7 , pointwise=TRUE )$WAIC
waic_m6.8 <- WAIC( m6.8 , pointwise=TRUE )$WAIC
n <- length(waic_m6.7)
diff_m6.7_m6.8 <- waic_m6.7 - waic_m6.8
sqrt( n*var( diff_m6.7_m6.8 ) )

[1] 10.35785




The difference between the models is 40.9 and the standard error about 10.4. If we imagine the 99% (corresponding to a z-score of about 2.6) interval of the difference, it’ll be about:

40.0 + c(-1,1)*10.4*2.6

[1] 12.96 67.04


So yes, these models are very easy to distinguish by expected out-of-sample accuracy. Model m6.7 is a lot better. You might be able to see all of this better, if we plot the compare table:

plot(compare(m6.6, m6.7, m6.8))









filled points: in-sample deviance values
open points: WAIC values

Naturally, each model does better in-sample than it is expected to do out-of-sample

line segments: standard error of each WAIC
light gray line segment with triangle: standard error of the difference in WAIC between two models

WAIC cannot be used to infer causation. Says that m6.7 is the best, even though this one contained the post-treatment variable (pipe confound between treatment and outcome)

since fungus is more highly correlated with the outcome, a model using it is likely to predict better. WAIC did its job. It’s job is not to infer causation. It’s job is to guess predictive accuracy.
Does not mean WAIC/CV/PSIS are useless - provides useful measure of the expected improvement in prediction that comes from conditioning on the fungus

Comparing m6.6 (intercept only) to m6.8 (with treatment only)

WAIC treats the two models as quite similar. Difference of only 3 units of deviance

Calculate the SE of the difference:

set.seed(92)
waic_m6.6 <- WAIC( m6.6 , pointwise=TRUE )$WAIC
diff_m6.6_m6.8 <- waic_m6.6 - waic_m6.8
sqrt(n*var(diff_m6.6_m6.8))

[1] 4.858923


The compare table doesn’t show, but did calculate. Need the dSE slot of the return

set.seed(93)
compare(m6.6, m6.7,m6.8)@dSE

          m6.6     m6.7      m6.8
m6.6        NA 12.20638  4.934361
m6.7 12.206385       NA 10.426574
m6.8  4.934361 10.42657        NA



This matrix contains all of the pairwise difference standard errors for the models you compared.
Notice that the standard error of the difference for m6.6 and m6.8 is bigger than the difference itself. We really cannot easily distinguish these models on the basis of WAIC.
Does this mean that the treatment doesn’t work? Of course not. We know that it works. We simulated the data. And the posterior distribution of the treatment effect, bt in m6.8, is reliably positive. But it isn’t especially large. So it doesn’t do much alone to improve prediction of plant height. There are just too many other sources of variation.

This result just echoes the core fact about WAIC (and CV and PSIS): It guesses predictive accuracy, not causal truth. A variable can be causally related to an outcome, but have little relative impact on it, and WAIC will tell you that.


weight element of compare table

these values are traditional way to summarize relative support for each model - always sum to 1 within set of compared models
used in model averaging (family of methods for combining the predictions of multiple models



Ex 2: Outliers and other illusions
Divorce example from Ch 5, posterior predictions for a few States were hard to model (Idaho was an outlier).

Individual points like Idaho tend to be very influential in ordinary regression models

its Pareto k value is double the theoretical point at which variance becomes infinite (x=0.5)
WAIC penalty >2; the sum of all penalty terms usually equals total free parameters in model → here, 4 parameters and total penalty is 6
Outlier causing additional overfitting risk



What to do about outliers causing additional overfitting risk?

DON’T: drop outliers based only on SDs from the mean outcome value

a point can only be unexpected and highly influential in light of a model;
After you fit a model, the picture changes. If there are only a few outliers, and you are sure to report results both with and without them, dropping outliers might be okay.
But if there are several outliers and we really need to model them, what then?


Basic problem: Gaussian error model is easily surprised (have very thin tails → little probability mass give to observations far from the mean)

Many real phenomena have thicker tails with rare, extreme outcomes

not measurement errors, but real events containing info about natural processes


Robust Regression: indicates a linear model in which the influence of extreme observations is reduced

one way to use extreme observations and reduce their influence
Common approach: replace Gaussian model with Student’s t distribution


Student’s T distribution
Thicker-tailed distribution arising from a mixture of Gaussian distributions with different variances (which can thicken the tails)

generalized Student-t distribution has same mean µ and scale \(\sigma\) parameters as Gaussian, but also an extra shape parameter \(\nu\) that controls how thick the tails are

dstudent in rethinking package

Large \(\nu\) → Thin tails (converging in the limit \(\nu = \infty\) to a Gaussian distribution)
As \(\nu\) approached 1, tails get thicker and rare extreme observations occur often

When using robust regression, we don’t normally try to estimate \(\nu\) because there aren’t enough extreme observations to do so

Instead assume \(\nu\) is small (thick tails) in order to reduce the influence of outliers

Re-estimate the divorce model with Student-t distribution with \(\nu = 2\) (just replace dnorm with dstudent:

title: Lec4: Categories and Curves
text:
Discrete, unordered types
Want to stratify by category: fit a separate regression line for each category



How are height, weight, and sex causally related?
How are height, weight, and sex statistically weighted?



The causes aren’t in the data

H → W: the arrow does from height to weight because there are fewer interventions on height than on weight (you can change your diet, exercise, etc. to change your weight, but not height). Height necessarily influences weight.
S → H: human biology, height does not influence sex; but sex does
S → H: same as above







Weight is influenced by both height (directly) and sex (both directly and indirectly via H)



\[H = f_{H}(S)\]
\[W = f_{W}(H,S)\]
Indirect causes do not show up in generative functions
Unobserved causes are ignorable unless shared among generative causes (H, W, S)




# S=1 female; S=2 male 
sim_HW <- function(S,b,a){
  N <- length(S)
  H <- ifelse(S==1, 150, 160) + rnorm(N, 0, 5) # add Gaussian noise with variance of 25cm
  W <- a[S] + b[S]*H + rnorm(N,0,5) 
  data.frame(S,H,W)
}

S <- rbern(100) + 1 # 100 individuals with male and female drawn at random 
dat <- sim_HW(S, b=c(0.5, 0.6), a=c(0,0)) 
# both alphas are zero - no sex effect on intercept
# slightly diff slopes: 0.5 for women, 0.6 for men 

head(dat)






Q: Causal effect on H on W? ← Already did this in last lecture
Q: Causal effect of S on W?

involves two sub-causes, direct and indirect

Q: Direct causal effect of S on W?

only direct cause = different stat model


Need to stratify by S: different estimate for each value S can take. How?









NoteCoding categorical variables




Indicator (0/1) variables
Index variables: 1,2,3,4

One of the sexes becomes the default, while the other becomes the adjustment



We will use index variables

Extend to many categories with no change in code
Better for specifying priors
Extend effortlessly to multilevel models


Vector of parameters, with index
\[\alpha_{S[i]}\]
\[\alpha = [\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}]\]


Statistical Model
\[W_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(µ_{i}, \sigma)\]
\[µ_{i} = \alpha_{s[i]}\]
Our priors:
\[\alpha_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(60,10)\]
\[\sigma \sim {\sf Uniform}(0,10)\]


What is the total causal effect of sex? Causal effect of sex = difference made intervening (i.e., mean male weight - mean female weight)

# Female sample 
S <- rep(1,100)
simF <- sim_HW(S, b=c(0.5,0.6), a=c(0,0))

# Male sample 
S <- rep(2,100)
simM <- sim_HW(S, b=c(0.5,0.6), a=c(0,0))

# Effect of sex (male - female)
mean(simM$W - simF$W)


When we test the estimator, these are the sample values we want to find

Now run the estimator and synthetic sample

# Observe samples - list of 1s or 2s, for females or males 
S <- rbern(100) + 1 # BTW, the +1 is because R is 1-indexed, rbern creates list of 0s,1s 
dat <- sim_HW(S,b=c(0.5,0.6), a=c(0,0))

# Estimate posterior 
m_SW <- quap(
  alist(
    W ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a[S],
    a[S] ~ dnorm(60,10),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
  ), data=dat
)
precis(m_SW, depth=2)


Difference between a[1] and a[2] is the estimate we’re looking for: the total causal effect (indirect and direct)
E.g., 97-75 = 22





d <- Howell1
d <- d[d$age>=18,]
dat <- list(
  W = d$weight,
  S = d$male + 1 ) #S = 1 female; S =2 male

m_SW <- quap(
  alist(
    W ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a[S],
    a[S] ~ dnorm(60,10),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
  ), data=dat
)





The unknowns themselves, a[1] and a[2], are not what we want; we have to do comparisons between these posterior distributions
The diff of mean weight is not in the posterior, the mean weight of each category is. But we’d like to look at the contrast between category 1 and 2
Need to use whole posterior distribution


par(mfrow=c(1,2))

# posterior mean W
post <- extract.samples(m_SW)
dens(post$a[,1], xlim=c(39,50), lwd=3, col=2, xlab="posterior mean weight (kg") 
dens(post$a[,2], lwd=3, col=4, add=TRUE)

# posterior W distributions, need to include SDs
W1 <- rnorm(1000,post$a[,1], post$sigma)
W2 <- rnorm(1000, post$a[,2], post$sigma)
dens(W1, xlim=c(20,70), ylim=c(0,0.085), lwd=3, col=2)
dens(W2, lwd=3, col=4, add=TRUE)


The densities of the means don’t overlap at all - indication that they’re reliably different







NoteAlways be contrasting




Contrast is often what we want, the difference between categories
It’s never legitimate to compare overlap in distributions - in parameters or lines

Overlap doesn’t reliably tell you much; the difference is reliably the same??
This means no comparing confidence intervals or p-values either

Must compute contrast distribution







str(post)

#causal contrast (in means)
mu_contrast <- post$a[,2] - post$a[,1] # subtract a[1] from a[2]
dens(mu_contrast, xlim=c(3,10), lwd=3, col=1, xlab="posterior mean weight contrast (kg)")


Posterior distribution of difference: knowledge about the average weight difference in women and men in this sample - between 5 and 9, centered around a little less than 7kg





What bout individual people’s body weights? What’s the contrast between these distributions?


# causal contrast of weight 
W_contrast <- W2 - W1
dens(W_contrast, xlim=c(-25,35), lwd=3, col=1, xlab="posterior weight contrast (kg")

#proportion above zero, men heavier than women
sum(W_contrast>0)/1000

#proportion below zero, women heavier than men
sum(W_contrast<0)/1000
abline(v=0)


Most of the time, men are heavier than women in this population, though some overlap






Now we need to block association thru H
Need to stratify by H


S <- rbern(100)+1 # simulate sample of sexes
dat <- sim_HW(S, b=c(0.5,0.5), a=c(0,10)) #different alpha, assume +10kg for men - direct effect

plot(dat$H, dat$W, col=c("red","blue")[S], xlab="height(cm)", ylab="weight (kg)")

abline(v=mean(dat$H), h=mean(dat$W), lty=3)


indirect: H influences W differently (slopes)
Direct: W differs net any slope differences




Ignore sex for a moment, regression on weight from height

\[W_{i} \sim {\sf Normal}(µ_{i}, \sigma)\]
\[µ_{i} = \alpha + \beta(H_{i} - \overline{H})\]

Centering H makes it so that alpha is the average weight of a person with average height.
Centering makes it easier to define scientific priors for alpha

alpha = expected weight at the expected height

so when \(H_{i} = \overline{H}\) → \(\beta\) * 0 → beta/slope has no effect



Now let’s add sex
\[µ_{i} = \alpha_{S[i]} + \beta_{s[i]}(H_{i} - \overline{H})\]

\(S[i]\) sex of i-th person (1=female, 2=male)

\[\alpha = [\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}],  \beta = [\beta_{1},\beta_{2}]\]

Two intercepts and two slopes, one for each value in S





data("Howell1")
d <- Howell1
d <- d[d$age >= 18,]
dat <- list(
  W = d$weight,
  H = d$height,
  Hbar = mean(d$height),
  S = d$male + 1) 

m_SHW <- quap(
  alist(
    W ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a[S] + b[S]*(H-Hbar),
    a[S] ~ dnorm(60,10),
    b[S] ~ dunif(0,1),
    sigma ~ dunif(0,10)
  ), data=dat, 
  start = list(
    a = c(60, 60),
    b = c(0.4, 0.4),
    sigma = 6)
)

Contrasts at each height

Compute posterior predictive for women
Compute posterior predictive for men
Subject (2) from (1)
Plot distribution at each height


xseq <- seq(130,190, len=50)
plot(NULL, xlim=range(xseq), ylim=c(-6,8), xlab="height (cm)", ylab="weight contrast (F - M)")


muF <- 
  link(m_SHW, data=list(S=rep(1,50), H=xseq,Hbar=mean(d$height)))
  lines(xseq, apply(muF,2,mean), lwd=3, col=2)

muM <- 
  link(m_SHW, data=list(S=rep(2,50), H=xseq,Hbar=mean(d$height)))
  lines(xseq, apply(muM,2,mean), lwd=3, col=4)

mu_contrast <- muF - muM
for (p in c(0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,0.99))
  shade(apply(mu_contrast,2,PI,prob=p), xseq)
abline(h=0, lty=2)


Posterior distribution of differences of in expected weight at each height between men and women according to the model
Gravity’s around 0, not much difference at any height between men and women’s heights

Taller women tend to weigh more than men of the same height
Shorter men tend to weigh more than women of same height

Nearly all of the causal effect of sex on weight acts thru height

The weight contrast distribution straddles zero line
Mean differences in weight by sex, but that’s because men are taller


So, almost no DIRECT effect of sex on weight in this population






NoteSummary: Category variables




Easy to use with index coding
Use samples to compute relevant contrasts
Always summarize (mean, intervals) as the last step

Do not summarize first and then take a difference

Want mean difference and NOT difference of means

N <- 300
Z <- rbern(N) 
X <- rnorm(N, 2*Z-1) # Z=1 will be positive, Z=0 will be negative

abline(lm(Y~X), lwd=3) # Regression line for total sample, ignoring Z







# Stratefying by common cause

Fork Example

Why do regions of the USA with higher rates of marriage also have higher divorce rates?
M → D ?

Another variable: age at marriage

library(dagitty)
ldag5.1 <- dagitty("dag{
                   A -> D
                   A -> M
                   M -> D }")
coordinates(ldag5.1) <- list(x=c(M=0, A=1, D=2), y=c(D=0,A=1, M=0))
drawdag(ldag5.1)








Estimand: Causal effect of marriage rate on divorce rate
Fork: M ← A → D

To estimate causal effect of M, need to break the fork. By stratifying by A

What does it mean to stratify by a continuous variable?

It depends
How does A influence D? What is \(D=f(A,M)\)?
In linear regression:

\[D_i \sim {\sf Normal}(µ_i, \sigma)\]
\[µ_i=\alpha + \beta_mM_i + \beta_aA_i\]

Every value of A produces a different relationship between D and M
\(µ_i= (a + \beta_AA_i) + \beta_MM_i\)

Where \(a + \beta_AA_i\) is the intercept


Statistical Fork

To stratify by A (age at marriage), include as term in linear model
We are going to standardize the variables (convenient in linear regression)

standardize: make the mean 0 and divide by the SD
Computation works better
Easy to choose sensible priors


Prior Predictive Simulation

n <- 20 
a <- rnorm(n,0,0.2)
bM <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
bA <- rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)

plot(NULL, xlim=c(-2,2), ylim=c(-2,2),xlab="Median age of marriage (std)", ylab="Divorce rate (std)")

Aseq <- seq(-3.3, len=30)
for (i in 1:n) {
  mu <- a[i] + bA[i] * Aseq
}

for (i in 1:n) {
  mu <- a[i] + bA[i] * Aseq
  lines(Aseq, mu, lwd=2, col=2)
}








Analyze Data

# create data list with standardized vals 
dat <- list(
  D = standardize(d$Divorce),
  M = standardize(d$Marriage),
  A = standardize(d$MedianAgeMarriage)
)

m_DMA <- quap(
  alist(
    D ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bA * A + bM * M,
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bM ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    bA ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=dat
)
plot(precis(m_DMA))








plot(precis(model_name)) Caterpillar Plot - good for visualizing summary of model with standardized variables

What’s the causal effect of M?

Just because the interval of M var includes zero does not mean that the causal effect of M is zero!
People will often report the slope of M as the causal effect of M, which is not terrible, but it’s not actually right. In a perfectly linear model. But nonlinear models complicate things.

bA is quite negative, though same level of uncertainty in both slopes (bA and bM)

Simulating Interventions

Causal effect is a manipulation of the generative model, an intervention
\(p(D|do(M)\) means the distribution of D when we intervene (“do”) M
This implies deleting all arrows into M and simulating D


ldag5.2 <- dagitty("dag{
                   A -> D
                  
                   M -> D }")
coordinates(ldag5.2) <- list(x=c(M=0, A=1, D=2), y=c(D=0,A=1, M=0))
drawdag(ldag5.2)









# Extract samples from the model 
post <- extract.samples(m_DMA)

# Sample A from the data, the empirically observed median age of marriage vals with Replacement 
# 1000 states 
n <- 1e3
As <- sample(dat$A, size=n, replace=TRUE)

# Simulate D for M=0 (sample mean)
DM0 <- with(post, # with makes it so we don't have to use $ to access columns 
            rnorm(n, a + bM*0 + bA*As, sigma))

# Simulate D for M=1 (+1 SD), use the *same* A values 
DM1 <- with(post, 
            rnorm(n, a + bM*1 + bA * As, sigma))

# Compute the constrast 
M10_contrast <- DM1 - DM0 
dens(M10_contrast, lwd=4, col=2, xlab="effect of 1SD increase in M")









Posterior distribution of the causal effect of intervening on M to inc it by one standard deviation on divorce rate. Centered on Zero, but could be big or small → can’t say that there’s no effect (variability on population error)

But certainly it’s a much smaller effect that the causal effect of A on D
Need to run another model


Causal effect of A?

How to estimate causal effect of A, \(p(D|do(A))\)

No arrows to delete for intervention
Fit new model that ignores M, then simulate any intervention you like

Why does ignoring M work?

Because A → M → D is a “pipe” (remember from last lecture with the Howell weight, age, height data)

Collider Examples
Some biases arise from selection (data collection)

Suppose: 200 grant applications

Each scored on newsworthiness and trustworthiness
No association in population
Strong association after selection:

negative association in the funded grants between trustworthiness and newsworthiness: the most newsworthiness have below average rigor in this applicant pool
But not a feature of how grants are written, but a feature of selection (once you stratify by whether it was funded or not)



\[N \rightarrow A \leftarrow T\]

Awarded grants must have been sufficiently newsworthy and trustworthy. Few grants are high in both. Results in a negative association, conditioning on award
Similar examples:

restaurants survive by having good food or a good location => bad food in good locations

Restaurants must survive by either one of two ways: have good food, or good location. (can be both, but pretty rare)
Induce slight conditioning on collider (nothing about being in a bad neighborhood that makes the food good)

Actors can succeed by being attractive or by being skilled => attractive actors are less skilled (selection bias of seeing only those actors that succeed, being attractive is not causally related to being bad at acting).


Endogenous Colliders

Collider bias can arise thru statistical processing (e.g., how you define the estimator)
Endogenous selection: if you condition on (stratify by) a collider, creates phantom non-causal associations
Example: Does age influence happiness?

Age and Happiness

Estimand: Influence of age on happiness
Possible confound: Marital status
Suppose age has zero influence on happiness
But both age and happiness influence marital status (happier people more likely to be married, older you are, the more chances of marriage)

\[H \rightarrow M \leftarrow A\]

Stratified by marital status, negative association between age and happiness

If you included marital status in your estimator as a control, it would in fact induce a confound: a negative association between age and happiness (just not true)

title: Lec 6: Good and Bad Controls
text:
Controls
control variable: variable introduced to an analysis so that a causal estimate is possible
Wrong heuristics for choosing control variables:

anything goes
any variables not highly collinear
Any pre-treatment measurement (baseline)











\(X → Y\) frontdoor and closed
\(X ← u → Z ← v → Y\) backdoor and closed

\(Z\) is collider
Remains closed as long as we don’t condition on \(Z\)
Not safe











X: win lottery
Y: Lifespan
Z: Happiness
u: contextual confounds
Conditioning on \(u\) is harmless UNLESS you try to stratify by \(Z\)! You can estimate the total causal effect of winning the lottery, but not direct causal effect.

Post-treatment variables are often risky controls


\(X → Z → Y\)
\(X → Z ← u → Y\)






Note



No backdoor path, no need to control for Z!!!



Simulate the DAG
Assume all arrows have effect of 1:

f <- function(n=100, bXZ=1, bZY=1){
  X <- rnorm(n)
  u <- rnorm(n)
  Z <- rnorm(n, bXZ*X + u)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bZY*Z + u)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean",xlim=c(-1,2), ylim=c(0,2.75))
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)









Adding Z in Y ~ X + Z makes it look like the effect is negative because it activates the confound
Y ~ X is correctly centered on 1.0

Now, assume all are 1 except bZY = 0 :

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(bZY=0), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean",xlim=c(-1,0.5), ylim=c(0,3))
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)









Again, Y ~ X is correctly centered on 0 (\(X\) has no causal influence on \(Y\) )
While Y ~ X + Z mistakenly shows a negative relationship







Note



Statistical significance is not a guide to model structure.



Colliders






Note



Do not touch the collider! Colliders are BAD CONTROLS


Colliders are not always obvious:










Z becomes a collider if you consider the possibility of unmeasured causes between Z and Y

X: education
Y: income
Z: values
u: family
EX: How does education affect income? Imagine you have data on people’s values based on survey results, so you decide to condition on values (Z). But, you could be conditioning on a collider and accidentally get estimates that are higher SPURIOUS. Because values are often associated with family/upbringing (u), which can be associated with income (Y).


Non-backdoor examples

Case-control bias (selection on the outcome)
\[X (education) → Y (occupation) → Z (Income) \]

If you stratify based on income (Z), you’re weakly stratifying on the occupation Y, the outcome itself. It narrows the range of occupations that experiences a narrower range of education levels (false inferences)

Let’s see a simulation of this: (assume all arrows have coefficient of 1)

f <- function(n=100, bXY=1, bYZ=1){
  X <- rnorm(n)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bXY*X)
  Z <- rnorm(n, bYZ*Y)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean",xlim=c(0,1.5), ylim=c(0,5))
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)









Conditioning on \(Z\) gives a weaker association (by half)



Precision parasite

Stratifying on the parent of X
\[Z → X → Y \]

Simulate the DAG

f <- function(n=100, bZX=1, bXY=1){
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  X <- rnorm(n, bZX*Z)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bXY*X)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean")
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)









Centers on the correct value, but it inflates the uncertainty (wider distribution)



Bias amplification

X and Y confounded by u
Something truly awful happens when we add Z

double activates the confound











X: occupation
Y: income
Z: education
u: regional/cultural factors
EX: Examining the association between occupation and income. Lots of regional and cultural factors that influences both. Stratifying by education seems reasonable… but this is a bias amplification problem.
Simulate: assume bXY is 0

f <- function(n=100, bZX=1, bXY=1){
  Z <- rnorm(n)
  u <- rnorm(n)
  X <- rnorm(n, bZX*Z + u)
  Y <- rnorm(n, bXY*X + u)
  bX <- coef(lm(Y ~ X))['X']
  bXZ <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z))['X']
  return(c(bX,bXZ))
}

sim <- mcreplicate(1e4, f(bXY=0), mc.cores = 8)

dens(sim[1,], lwd=3, xlab="posterior mean")
dens(sim[2,], lwd=3, col=2, add=TRUE)









Real value is 0 (no association between X and Y)… but the model finds association
The default model is already biased (we knew that - just the effect of an unobserved confound)
Conditioning on Z increases the bias

Why?

Covariation between X and Y can only exist if there’s variation in their causes

The cause of Y is X, and if X doesn’t vary then Y can’t vary
Then Z is a cause of X… so if Z doesn’t vary then X can’t vary

Within each level of Z, there is less variation in X

When we stratify by Z, we remove the variation in Z that causes X
Therefore the covariation between X and Y must be smaller within each level of Z

Consequently, confound \(u\) becomes relatively more important within each Z (when we condition on Z)

When you average across the levels of Z, you find more association between X and Y



n <- 1000 
Z <- rbern(n) # make Z binary to make viz of stratification easier (either 0 or 1)
u <- rnorm(n)
X <- rnorm(n, 7*Z + u)
Y <- rnorm(n, 0*X + u)

# looking for a slope of 0 = no association 







Note



Control variable: variable introduced to an analysis so that a causal estimate is possible
Heuristics fail – adding control variables can be worse than omitting
Make assumptions explicit (must do scientific modeling [DAGs] to do scientific data analysis)

title: Ch 6: The Haunted DAG & The Causal Terror
text:
Multicollinearity
When there’s a very strong correlation between two or more of the predictor variables, the posterior distribution will seem to suggest that none of the variables are associated with the outcome, even if all the variables are actually strongly associated with the outcome

Example 1: Using leg length to predict height

Multicollinearity occurs when you put the lengths of both legs in the model


N <- 100 # number of individuals 
set.seed(909)
height <- rnorm(N, 10, 2) # sim total height of each 
leg_prop <- runif(N, 0.4, 0.5) # leg as proportion of height 
leg_left <- leg_prop*height + rnorm(N,0,0.02) # left leg as propotion + error 
leg_right <- leg_prop*height + rnorm(N,0,0.02)

d <- data.frame(height, leg_left, leg_right)

What we’d expect: on average legs are 45% of height (in these simulated data) → the beta coefficient that measures the association of a leg with height should be the avg height (10) divided by 45% of the avg height (4.5), which is \(10/4.5 \approx 2.2\).
Using vague priors, run a model to approximate the posterior:

m6.1 <- quap(
  alist(
    height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bl*leg_left + br*leg_right,
    a ~ dnorm(10,100),
    bl ~ dnorm(2, 10),
    br ~ dnorm(2, 10),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), 
  data=d
)
precis(m6.1)

           mean        sd       5.5%    94.5%
a     0.9811946 0.2839605  0.5273710 1.435018
bl    0.2138690 2.5270778 -3.8248894 4.252627
br    1.7816829 2.5312914 -2.2638096 5.827175
sigma 0.6171136 0.0434362  0.5476942 0.686533



plot(precis(m6.1))








Why is the posterior distribution so weird?

Multiple linear regression answers the question: what is the value of knowing each leg’s length, after already knowing the other leg’s length?

Look at the bivariate posterior distribution for bl and br

post <- extract.samples(m6.1)
plot(bl ~ br, post, col=col.alpha(rangi2, 0.1), pch=16)









the posterior distribution is very highly correlated. When bl is large, then br must be small
Since both leg variables contain almost exactly the same information, if you insist on including both in the model, then there will be a practically infinite number of combinations of bl and br that produce the same predictions

Think about it this way: we approximated the model below
\[y_i \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma) \]
\[\mu_i = \alpha + \beta_1x_i + \beta_2x_i\]
y is the outcome (height) and x is a single predictor (like leg lengths, almost identical values). From computer’s pov, this is
\[\mu_i = \alpha + (\beta_1 + \beta_2)x_i\]
The betas cannot be pulled apart as they don’t separately influence the mean µ; only their sum, \(\beta_1 + \beta_2\), influences \(\mu\). As a result, the posterior distribution reports a very large range of combinations of \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) hat make their sum close to the actual association of x and y.

sum_blbr <- post$bl + post$br
dens(sum_blbr, col=rangi2, lwd=2, xlab="sum of bl and br")









what the previous posterior distribution in the simulated example did was produce a good estimate of the sum of br and bl.
The posterior mean is in the right neighborhood (a little over 2) and the SD is smaller than it is for either component of the sum individually.

So if you fit the regression with only one of the leg length variables, you get approximately the same posterior mean as the sum:

m6.2 <- quap(
  alist(
    height ~ dnorm(mu, sigma), 
    mu <- a + bl*leg_left,
    a ~ dnorm(10,100), 
    bl ~ dnorm(2,10), 
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data = d
)

precis(m6.2)

           mean         sd      5.5%    94.5%
a     0.9979320 0.28364620 0.5446105 1.451253
bl    1.9920678 0.06115704 1.8943271 2.089809
sigma 0.6186037 0.04353998 0.5490184 0.688189



When two predictor variables are very strongly correlated, including both in a model may lead to confusion.
The posterior distribution isn’t wrong though, but it cannot make claims about which of the two predictor variables is more important.



Example 2: primate milk data

data(milk)
d <- milk 
d$K <- scale(d$kcal.per.g)
d$F <- scale(d$perc.fat)
d$L <- scale(d$perc.lactose)

Model kcal.per.g as function of perc.fat and perc.lactose in two bivariate regressions

# kcal.per.g regressed on perc.fat 

m6.3 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bF*F, 
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bF ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data = d
)

# kcal.per.g regressed on perc.lactose 
m6.4 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bL*L, 
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bL ~ dnorm(0, 0.5), 
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)

precis(m6.3)

              mean         sd       5.5%     94.5%
a     1.535525e-07 0.07725195 -0.1234634 0.1234637
bF    8.618970e-01 0.08426088  0.7272318 0.9965621
sigma 4.510179e-01 0.05870756  0.3571919 0.5448440

precis(m6.4)

               mean         sd       5.5%      94.5%
a      7.438824e-07 0.06661633 -0.1064650  0.1064665
bL    -9.024550e-01 0.07132848 -1.0164517 -0.7884583
sigma  3.804653e-01 0.04958259  0.3012227  0.4597078



posterior distributions for bF and bL are mirror images of each other (positive vs negative slope; narrow distributions on one side of 0)

Putting both as predictor variables in a regression model:

m6.5 <- quap(
  alist(
    K ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- a + bL*L + bF*F, 
    a ~ dnorm(0,0.2),
    bL ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),

Density of milk → tradeoff between lactose and fat levels in milk

title: Ch 6: The Haunted DAG & The Causal Terror
text:
Post-treatment bias

Example: Plant fungus treatment
Investigating the difference in plant growth under varying anti-fungal soil treatments. Initial plant heights measured before treatments applied. Final measures are height of plant and presence of fungi.

Four variables: initial height, final height (outcome of interest), treatment, and presence of fungus
Model should NOT include the fungus presence variables, because it’s the post-treatment effect


set.seed(71)
N <- 100 

# simulate initial heights 
h0 <- rnorm(N,10,2)

# assign treatments and simulate fungus & growth
treatment <- rep(0:1, each=N/2)
fungus <- rbinom(N,size=1, prob=0.5 - treatment*0.4)
h1 <- h0 + rnorm(N,5 - 3*fungus)

# compose a clean data frame 
d <- data.frame(h0=h0, h1=h1, treatment=treatment, fungus=fungus)
precis(d)

              mean        sd      5.5%    94.5%    histogram
h0         9.95978 2.1011623  6.570328 13.07874 ▁▂▂▂▇▃▂▃▁▁▁▁
h1        14.39920 2.6880870 10.618002 17.93369     ▁▁▃▇▇▇▁▁

fungus     0.23000 0.4229526  0.000000  1.00000   ▇▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂



IGNORE this data generating process (wouldn’t actually know how the data is generated irl)

Focusing on the height variables: final height should be taller than initial heights, regardless of scale → put the parameters on the scale of proportion of height at time t=0 to set the priors more easily
Linear model
\[h_{1,i} \sim {\sf Normal}(\mu_i,\sigma)\]
\[\mu_i = h_{0,i} \times p\]
\(h_{0,i}\) is plant \(i\)’s height at time \(t=0\), \(h_{1,i}\) is height at time \(t=1\), and \(p\) is a parameter measuring the proportion of \(h_{0,i}\) that \(h_{1,i}\) is.
Setting the prior for \(p\):

Allow \(p\) to be less than 1, in the case the plants die
Ensure \(p > 0\) since p is a proportion
Use Log-Normal distribution, since it’s always positive

\[p \sim {\sf Log-Normal}(0,0.25)\]

sim_p <- rlnorm(1e4, 0,0.25)
precis(data.frame(sim_p))

         mean        sd     5.5%    94.5%    histogram
sim_p 1.03699 0.2629894 0.670683 1.496397 ▁▁▃▇▇▃▁▁▁▁▁▁



this prior expects anything from 40% shrinkage to 50% growth


m6.6 <- quap(
  alist(
    h1 ~ dnorm( mu , sigma ),
    mu <- h0*p,
    p ~ dlnorm( 0 , 0.25 ),
    sigma ~ dexp( 1 )
  ), data=d )

sigma 1.793286 0.12517262 1.593236 1.993336



about 40% growth on average

Adding other variables into the model
Post treatment bias (don’t do this):

If you include the treatment AND fungus variables… parameters will also be in proportion scale (changes in proportion growth).

using flat priors that place 95% of the prior mass between -1 (100% reduction) and +1 (100% increase) and two-thirds of the prior mass between -0.5 and +0.5.



m6.7 <- quap(
  alist(
    h1 ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- h0*p,
    p <- a + bt*treatment + bf*fungus,
    a ~ dlnorm(0,0.2),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    bf ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d
)

the marginal posterior for bt is solidly 0 with a tight interval = treatment not associated with growth
fungus seems to have hurt growth

problem: fungus is mostly a consequence of treatment
the model is basically asking: once we already know whether or not a plant developed fungus, does soil treatment matter? (no)


Omit the post-treatment variable fungus:

m6.8 <- quap(
  alist(
    h1 ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- h0*p,
    p <- a + bt*treatment,
    a ~ dlnorm(0,0.2),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)

Treatment’s impact is clearly positive

The fact that including fungus zeros the coefficient for treatment suggests that the treatment works for exactly the anticipated reasons. It tells us about mechanism. But a correct inference about the treatment still depends upon omitting the post-treatment variable.
post-treatment bias can fool you into thinking the treatment doesn’t work


Fungus and d-separation

library(dagitty)
plant_dag <- dagitty( "dag {
  H_0 -> H_1
  F -> H_1
  T -> F
}")
coordinates( plant_dag ) <- list( x=c(H_0=0,T=2,F=1.5,H_1=1) ,
                                  y=c(H_0=0,T=0,F=0,H_1=0) )
drawdag( plant_dag )









When F is included in the model, the path from treatment T to outcome H1 is blocked. Learning the treatment tells us nothing about the outcome, once we know the fungus status.
Conditioning on \(F\) induces d-separation

d for “directional”
some variables on the directed graph are independent of others (no path connecting them)

\(H_1\) is \(d\)-separated from \(T\), but only when we condition on \(F\)
There is no info in \(T\) about \(H_1\) that is not also in \(F\). So once we know \(F\), learning \(T\) offers no additional info about \(H_1\)
implied conditional independencies




impliedConditionalIndependencies(plant_dag)

F _||_ H_0
H_0 _||_ T
H_1 _||_ T | F



The original plant height should not be associated with the treatment or fungus, provided we do not condition on anything

Post-treatment bias can also make us think that the treatment does work when it doesn’t

For example, let M be the unobserved variable for moisture levels. It influences both \(H_1\) and \(F\).

A regression of \(H_1\) on \(T\) will show no association between the treatment and plant growth, but including \(F\) in the model will show an association



set.seed(71)
N <- 1000
h0 <- rnorm(N,10,2)

  alist(
    h1 ~ dnorm(mu, sigma),
    mu <- h0*p,
    p <- a + bt*treatment + bf*fungus,
    a ~ dlnorm(0,0.2),
    bt ~ dnorm(0,0.5),
    bf ~ dnorm(0,0.5),

  ), data=d2  #new data from d2
)

sigma 2.10262855 0.04694249 2.02760537 2.17765172

Model m6.7 misleads because it asks the wrong question, not because it would make poor predictions. As argued in Chapter 1, prediction and causal inference are just not the same task. No statistical procedure can substitute for scientific knowledge and attention to it. We need multiple models because they help us understand causal paths, not just so we can choose one or another for prediction.

title: Ch 6: The Haunted DAG & The Causal Terror
text:
Collider bias
DAG model: trustworthiness ( \(T\)) and newsworthiness ( \(N\)) are statistically independent in the population research proposals submitted to grant review panels. Both of them influence selection ( \(S\)) for funding

grant_dag <- dagitty( "dag {
  T -> S
  N -> S
}")
coordinates( grant_dag ) <- list( x=c(T=0,S=0.5,N=1) ,
                                  y=c(T=0,S=0,N=0) )
drawdag( grant_dag )








A collider has two arrows pointing to it

When you condition a collider, it creates statistical, but not necessarily causal, associations among its causes

Once you learn that a proposal has been selected, then learning its trustworthiness can also tell you something about its newsworthiness. For example, if a selected proposal is low on trustworthiness, it must have high newsworthiness, or else it wouldn’t have been selected

If you include the collider as a predictor variable → misleading associations inside statistical model, may make erroneous causal inference


Example 1: aging and happiness
Is age associated with happiness in a large survey? If so, is the association causal?

This example will show that controlling for a possible confound for happiness can actually bias inference about the influence of age

Happiness (H) and age (A) both influence marriage, so marriage (M) is a collider. If we condition on marriage (include M as a predictor variable in the regression model) then it will induce a statistical association between age and happiness.
Agent-based simulation of data to use in regression






Note



Simulation design:

Each year, 20 people are born with uniformly distributed happiness values.
Each year, each person ages one year. Happiness does not change.
At age 18, individuals can become married. The odds of marriage each year are proportional to an individual’s happiness.
Once married, an individual remains married
After age 65, individuals leave the sample. (They move to Spain.)




# simulation algorithm included in package
library(rethinking)

# run it out for 1000 years and collect data
d <- sim_happiness(seed = 1977, N_years = 1000)
precis(d)

                  mean        sd      5.5%     94.5%     histogram
age       3.300000e+01 18.768883  4.000000 62.000000 ▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇
married   3.007692e-01  0.458769  0.000000  1.000000    ▇▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▃
happiness 6.832142e-19  1.214421 -1.789474  1.789474      ▇▅▇▅▅▇▅▇



At age 18, they become able to marry, and then gradually more individuals are married each year. So at older ages, more individuals are married. But at all ages, the happiest individuals are more likely to be married.

Haunted DAG

Unmeasured causes can also induce collider bias (haunted)



Example 2: Familial Educational Achievement
Inferring the direct influence of both parents (P) and grandparents (G) on educational achievement of children (C).

Presumably, G also influences C
Unmeasured common influences: neighborhoods (not shared by G)

haunted by unobserved U

So P becomes common consequence of G and U… if we condition on P, it will bias inference about G → C, even if we never get to measure U.

Simulate 200 triads of grandparents, parents, and children

N <- 200 # number of grandparent-parent-child triads
b_GP <- 1 # direct effect of G on P
b_GC <- 0 # direct effect of G on C
b_PC <- 1 # direct effect of P on C
b_U <- 2 # direct effect of U on P and C


These parameters are like slopes in a regression model, use these slopes to draw random observations


set.seed(1)
U <- 2*rbern( N , 0.5 ) - 1 # binary effect
G <- rnorm( N )
P <- rnorm( N , b_GP*G + b_U*U )
C <- rnorm( N , b_PC*P + b_GC*G + b_U*U )
d <- data.frame( C=C , P=P , G=G , U=U )


# Normally would standardize priors, but easier to see what happens without 
m6.11 <- quap(
  alist(
    C ~ dnorm( mu , sigma ),
    mu <- a + b_PC*P + b_GC*G,
    a ~ dnorm(0, 1),
    c(b_PC,b_GC) ~ dnorm(0, 1),
    sigma ~ dexp(1)
  ), data=d )
precis(m6.11)

a     -0.1174752 0.09919574 -0.2760091  0.04105877
b_PC   1.7868915 0.04455355  1.7156863  1.85809664
b_GC  -0.8389537 0.10614045 -1.0085867 -0.66932077
sigma  1.4094891 0.07011139  1.2974375  1.52154063



When conditioning on the parents, a negative association arises between G and C.

like looking within sub-populations of parents with similar education
once we know P, learning G invisibly tells us about the neighborhood U, and U is associated with the outcome C.
Consider 2 different parents with same education level. One of the paretns has a highly educated grandparent, the other has poorly educated grandparent. The only probable way, in this examplpe, for these parents to have the same education is if they live in different types of neighborhoods. We can’t see the neighborhood effects, but it is transmitted to the children.

So for the two parents with same education, the one with the highly educated grandparent ends up with a less educated child. The one with the less educated grandparent ends up with a better educated child. G predicts lower C.



Have to measure U since it makes P a collider.

title: Ch 6: The Haunted DAG & The Causal Terror
text:
Confronting Confounding
Why does multiple regression sometimes deal with confounding, and sometimes lead to confounding (controlling the wrong variables)?
Confounding: any context in which the association between an outcome Y and a predictor of interest X is not the same as it would be if we had experimentally determined the values of X (blocked out non-causal paths)
Suppose we’re interested on education’s (E) association with wages (W). In a typical population, there are many unobserved variables that influence both E and W.









Paths from E to W

\(E → W\) (Causal)
\(E ← U → W\) (Non-causal)

path: any series of variables you could walk through to get from one variable to another, ignoring the directions of the arrows
Traditional way to isolate the causal path = run an experiment (manipulate the predictor)
Assign educational levels at random to remove the influence of \(U\) on \(E\). The unobserved variables do not influence education when we ourselves determine education.









This blocks the path \(E ← U → W\)
Statistical Method to Block Non-Causal paths (without manipulating predictor)
Add \(U\) to the model = condition on \(U\). This blocks the flow of info from E and W through U.

Once you learn U, also learning E is redundant (to learn about W).
Ex: if U is the average wealth in the region, U affects E (more education) and W (higher paying jobs). If nothing is known about person’s location, then knowing E can provide info about W. But when you know the location (assuming no other path between E and W), then learning E tells nothing about W.
I.e., conditioning on U blocks the path, making E and W independent, conditional on U.

shutting the backdoor: blocking all confounding paths between some predictor and some outcome Y.

avoiding spurious correlations sneaking in thru non-causal path (one that enters the back of the predictor X)







Note




Fork

X ← Z → Y
Classic confounder: some variable Z is a common cause of X and Y, generating a correlation between them. If we condition on Z, then learning X tells us nothing about Y. X and Y are independent, conditional on Z.

Pipe

X → Z → Y
Seen in the plant growth example and post-treatment bias: the treatment X influences fungus Z which influences growth Y. If we condition on Z now, we also block the path from X to Y. So in both a fork and a pipe, conditioning of the middle variable blocks the path.

Collider

X → Z ← Y
In a collider, there is no association between X and Y unless you condition on Z. Conditioning on Z, the collider variable, opens the path. Once the path is open, info flows between X and Y.

Descendent

Conditioning on a descendant variable is like conditioning on the variable itself, but weaker. A descendant variable is influenced by another variable. Controlling for D will also control, to a lesser extent, Z. (D has some info about Z). This will partially open the path from X to Y, because Z is a collider.
Same holds for non-colliders. If you condition on a descendant of Z in the pipe, it’ll still be like weakly closing the pipe.




Figure out which variables you need to control or not in order to shut the backdoor.






NoteRecipe




List all of the paths connecting X (the potential cause of interest) and Y (the outcome)
Classify each path by whether it is open or closed. A path is open unless it contains a collider
Classify each path by whether it is a backdoor path. A backdoor path has an arrow entering X.
If there are any backdoor paths that are also open, decide which variable(s) to condition on to close it




Example: Two Roads

dag_6.1 <- dagitty( "dag {
  U [unobserved]
  X -> Y
  X <- U <- A -> C -> Y
  U -> B <- C
}")
coordinates( dag_6.1 ) <- list( x=c(A=2, U=1, C=3, B=2, X=1, Y=3) ,
                                  y=c(A=1.5, U=2, C=2, B=2.5, X=3, Y=3) )
drawdag( dag_6.1 )








(1) List all paths connecting X and Y

\(X ← U ← A → C → Y\)
\(X ← U → B ← C → Y\)

(2) Classify whether path is open or closed

Path 1 is open because there is no collider variable (just fork and pipes on each side)
Path 2 is closed because there is a collider variable B (and two pipes)

(3) Classify whether path is a backdoor path or not

Both Paths 1 is backdoor path because they have arrows entering X

(4) If there are any backdoor paths that are also open, decide which variable(s) to condition on to close it
Just focusing on Path 1 (open backdoor) for now

Cannot condition on U bc it’s unobserved
Thus, either A or C will shut the back door

Ask computer to analyze the graph and find the necessary variables to control for in order to block the backdoor. dagitty R package provides adjustmentSets for this:



adjustmentSets( dag_6.1 , exposure="X" , outcome="Y" )

{ C }
{ A }



Conditioning on C may be better/more efficient - could help with the precision of the estimate of \(X → Y\).

Conditioning on \(U\) would also work, but since we told dagitty that \(U\) is unobserved, it didn’t suggest it.


Now, the Path 2, a closed path (B is a collider variable). It is not a backdoor, thus adjustmentSets doesn’t mention \(B\).

Do not need to control for \(B\). (might lead to faulty inferences if you do).



Example: Backdoor waffles
Total causal effect of the number of Waffle Houses on divorce rate in each state

dag_6.2 <- dagitty("dag{
                   S -> A
                   S -> M 
                   S -> W 
                   A -> D
                   A -> M 
                   M -> D
                   W -> D }")
coordinates( dag_6.2 ) <- list( x=c(S=1, A=1, M=1.5, W=2, D=2) ,
                                y=c(S=1, A=2, M=1.5, W=1, D=2) )
drawdag( dag_6.2 )








Assumptions in this graph:

\(S → A\): southern States have lower age of marriage
\(S → M\): southern States have higher rates of marriage both directly…
\(S → A → M\)… and indirectly through age of marriage
\(S → W\): southern States have more waffle houses
Age and marriage rate both influence divorce rate

(1) List all paths connecting W and D

\(W ← S → M → D\)
\(W ← S → M ← A → D\)
\(W ← S → A → M → D\)
\(W ← S → A → D\)

(2) Classify whether path is open or closed
(3) Classify whether path is a backdoor path or not

There are three open backdoor paths

(4) If there are any backdoor paths that are also open, decide which variable(s) to condition on to close it

adjustmentSets(dag_6.2, exposure = "W", outcome="D")

{ A, M }
{ S }



All pass first through S, can close them all by conditioning on S. Alternatively control for A and M.

This DAG assumes there are no unobserved confounds (unlikely).

Conditional independences: pairs of variables that are not associated once we condition on some set of other variables. Test some of the features of this graph by assessing each conditional independency.


impliedConditionalIndependencies(dag_6.2)

A _||_ W | S
D _||_ S | A, M, W
M _||_ W | S



“median age of marriage should be independent of Waffle Houses, conditioning on a State being in the south.”
“divorce and being in the south should be independent when we simultaneously condition on all of median age of marriage, marriage rate, and Waffle Houses.”
“Marriage rate and waffle houses should be independent when conditioning on a State being in the south”

Some important points about Bayesian Inference

There is no minimum sample size (minimum is 1)

Not informative, but accurately representing the relative confidence we should assign to each of the possible proportions.

Shape embodies sample size (all info about the generative process, proportion)

Post distribution embodies the sample size
When we observe more data, no need to go to original dataset, just take the post distribution and update it (where each possibility can produce new obs)

No point estimates: the posterior distribution is the point distribution

When we work with it, we’re working with the whole distribution everytime
Mode: max of the hill
Mean: central probability estimate
No point by itself is sufficient
when we compute things from the post distribution, we use the entire distribution, never a point from the distribution

No one true interval of the distribution

Intervals are unimportant.
merely quick summaries of the shape of posterior distribution

Confidence intervals - 50%, 89%, 99% (the lower and upper bounds)
nothing special happens at the boundary (arbitrary)
only thing 95% intervals try to do is reduce Type I error (significance testing), but that’s not what we’re trying to do here. We’re trying to estimate something.

Components of the model

Variables

Parameters: unobserved variables

target of inference, p, the proportion of water on the globe (the estimand defined)

Observed variables: counts of water and land

Likelihood: a distribution function assigned to an observed variable




Observed Variables

Binomial Distribution
The common “coin tossing” distribution. Assumptions that (1) every toss is independent of the other tosses and (2) the prob of W is the same on every toss

The counts of “water” W and “land” L are distributed binomially, with probability p of “water” on each toss

Binomial function is built into R (dbinom, or density binomial) Compute likelihood of the data (6 Ws in 9 tosses) under any value of p with:

dbinom(6, size=9, prob=0.5)

[1] 0.1640625


Maximum entropy: There are two events, and the probabilities of each in each trial are p and 1-p. 



Unobserved Variables
A Bayesian machine must have an initial plausibility (prior) assignment for each possible value of the parameter.
Where do priors come from? Engineering assumptions chosen to help the machine learn, and Scientific assumptions chosen to reflect what we know about the phenomenon.

Flat priors (when N=0) are common, but hardly the base prior
Can try out different priors when at a loss for a strong argument for any particular prior


Because the prior is an assumption, it should be interrogated like other assumptions: by altering it and checking how sensitive inference is to the assumption.



Summarize model
The observed vars W and l are given relative counts thru the binomial distribution. Shortcut: $ W ~ Binomial(N,p) $ where $ N = W + L \(. Assumption here is the relative counts of ways to realize W in N trials with probability p on each trial comes from the binomial distribution. And the unobserved parameter p similarly gets:\) p ~ Uniform(0,1) $ Which means that p has a uniform (FLAT) prior over its entire possible range, from 0 to one.

this is obviously not the best we could do, since we know the Earth has more water than land, even if we do not know the exact proportion yet.

text:
Bayes Theorem
Def of posterior distribution.
Joint prob of data W and L and any particular value of \(p\) is:
\(Pr(W, L, p) = Pr(W,L | p)Pr(p)\)

Probability of rain and cold on same day is equal to prob of rain, given it’s cold multiplied by the prob that it’s cold

Take the reverse: Probability of rain and cold on the same day is also equal to the prob of cold, given that it’s rainy, multiplied by the prob that it’s rainy.
\(Pr(W,L,p) = Pr(p|W,L)Pr(W,L)\)
These two defs equal each other so:
\(Pr(W,L | p)Pr(p) = Pr(p|W,L)Pr(W,L)\)
So to solve for \(Pr(p|W,L)\):
\(Pr(p|W,L) = \frac{Pr(W,L|p)Pr(p)}{Pr(W,L)}\)
What’s the weird thing in the denom? It;s the average probability of the data, which standardizes the posterior (ensure it sums to 1)
The posterior is proportional to the product of the prior and the probability of the data.

Fitting the Model

Grid approximation
Can get a great approx of continuous posterior with only a finite grid of parameter values
Mainly useful as pedagogical tool, but scales poorly when parameters INC.

# define grid
p_grid <- seq( from=0 , to=1 , length.out=20 )

# define prior
prior <- rep( 1 , 20 )

# compute likelihood at each value in grid
likelihood <- dbinom( 6 , size=9 , prob=p_grid )

#compute unstandardized posterior at each parameter value (product of likelihood and prior) 
unstd.posterior <- likelihood * prior

# standardize the posterior, so it sums to 1
posterior <- unstd.posterior / sum(unstd.posterior)

# DISPLAY 
plot(p_grid, posterior, type="b", xlab="prob of water", ylab ="posterior prob")









step_prior <- ifelse( p_grid < 0.5 , 0 , 1 )
plot(step_prior, type ="l")









Let’s try the prior where we assume a 0% chance of the true proportion of water being less than 50%

#define prior
step_prior <- ifelse( p_grid < 0.5 , 0 , 1 )

# compute likelihood at each value in grid

Let’s try that with a peaked prior that shifts and skews the posterior, relative to the likelihood.

#define prior
peaked_prior <- exp( -5*abs( p_grid - 0.5 ) )

plot(peaked_prior, type ="l")

Quadratic approximation
Under quite general conditions, the region near the peak of the posterior distribution will be nearly Gaussian—or “normal”—in shape. This means the posterior distribution can be usefully approximated by a Gaussian distribution. A Gaussian distribution is convenient, because it can be completely described by only two numbers: the location of its center (mean) and its spread (variance).

A Gaussian approximation is called “quadratic approximation” because the logarithm of a Gaussian distribution forms a parabola. And a parabola is a quadratic function. So this approximation essentially represents any log-posterior with a parabola.
